This research investigates the structure of $\mathbb{R}$-algebras that are both periodic and nonexpansive curve systems. We establish that for any positive real number $p$, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the equivalence classes of periodic algebras with period $P = p$ and monic degree $p$ Laurent polynomials with constant term 1, where the leading coefficient is positive. Furthermore, we demonstrate a specific scenario where the algebraic period $P$ is the square of the geometric period $P_{geo}$ of the associated nonexpansive curve; here, $P$ is the largest integer such that the curve admits a symmetry of order $P$ composed of translations of period $P_{geo}^2$. The paper also provides a complete classification of the cyclic subgroups of the isometry group $\mathit{Iso}(\mathbb{T})$ for the circle group $\mathit{Iso}(\mathbb{T})$, where each subgroup has an element of order $P$ representing a symmetry of order $P$ translations of period $P_{geo}^2$.

The widely used Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method identifies prominent spatial structures and their corresponding temporal behaviors within data, yet it remains vulnerable to significant shifts in a system's operating regime, which can drastically alter the meanings of these modes. While a prior approach called kernel DMD (kDMD) addressed this susceptibility by selecting modes based on temporal sparsity using kernel techniques, it suffered from the constraint that it could only handle scenarios where every single mode needed to be retained. This paper introduces a new version called LANDO (Linear and Nonlinear Adaption for DMD with a focus on Sparsity and pruninD), which prunes specific modes to enhance resilience against regime changes. Mode pruning is executed using a customized sparsity-promoting objective function that can be applied either to standard DMD or via kernel DMD. To execute this pruning, we developed a gradient-based optimization technique named education, forming the core of the LANDO algorithm. The effectiveness of this method is validated on both synthetic datasets and real-world data from a chemical reactor, demonstrating its capability to produce robust predictions even during substantial regime shifts.

This study introduces a novel metric for evaluating the similarity between chess openings by integrating concepts of path length and diameter within a graph framework. We analyze a dataset comprising approximately 3 million distinct openings sourced from Chess.com, leveraging site-specific popularity data to define metric properties. Our findings reveal that, when treated as a metric space, this collection of openings forms a deeply intricate structure with shallow depth, effectively creating a "chess opening wall." Furthermore, we introduce several new methods for both quantitative and qualitative assessing the similarity of these openings, ultimately suggesting an approach to revolutionizing how chess openings are organized.

The study of millisecond pulsars (MSPs) offers significant value for investigating neutron star properties. This research introduces a data-driven approach to automatically determine the key parameters required for detecting and characterizing pulsars within pale dwarf star systems. The methodology relies on model selection theory, specifically utilizing Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)-based techniques to identify periodic signals in both time and frequency domains across dwarf systems. The effectiveness of this approach was verified through a test case involving the binary system J0220+2100, where the method successfully recovered the known orbital period of 117.2 days and identified a previously unknown period of 2.91 hours. Additionally, when applied to dwarf systems lacking intrinsic pulsations, the approach successfully extracted neutron star parameters from the MSPs PSR J0437-4715 and PSR B1931+24. The findings confirm that this technique can reliably extract neutron star characteristics from dwarf binaries, including those that are only partially resolved.

This study examines quantities related to movement within both nonholonomic and holonomic frameworks, utilizing variations of the generalized virtual work principle alongside virtual displacements of arbitrary order. The analysis reveals the inherent irreducibility of these derived figures and their connection to the classical virtual work concept. Notably, the first-order irreducible quantity elucidates the fundamental structure of the principles governing the generalized virtual work. Moreover, irreducible forms in Lagrangian irreducible quantities of any degree facilitate the formulation of motion principles based on the Euler-Lagrange differential expressions raised to the corresponding power.

This study explores the potential of virtual reality (VR) drawing for retrieving information in three dimensions. The investigation centers on a new VR-drawing interface designed to capture user intent, translating their inputs into 3D VR-drawn objects. These generated models are then converted to volumetric data, which serves as a query mechanism to locate and retrieve 3D shapes from a repository. The system was evaluated through a study involving 10 participants who assessed its usability, following which a performance evaluation was also conducted to determine the system's overall effectiveness.

We present new, high-precision photometric measurements of the exoplanet HD 80606 b, derived from a global network of telescopes. By combining our data with existing light curves, we significantly improved the accuracy of the epoch ephemeris, reducing uncertainty from $ \pm 10^3 $ seconds to a record-breaking $\pm 2$ seconds. This level of precision is critical for planning JWST observations, particularly for timing future transit events. We also highlight that while the transiting nature of this system was only recently confirmed, the next predicted transit is estimated to have an uncertainty of $\pm 10$ seconds. Moving forward, maintaining this accuracy will require periodic re-measurements of the orbital period on timescales of decades to ensure reliable observation scheduling.

This study examines the collapse of a spherically symmetric, self-gravitating ideal fluid, adhering to a linear equation of states $p = (v_s^2\rho)/3 - p_c v_s$, where $v_s$ represents the sound velocity and $\rho$ is density. The analysis adheres to the principles of adiabatic dynamics, $\gamma = 4/3$, implying zero entropy variation. By integrating the Poisson equation for gravity with the equations of motion, a simplified ordinary differential equation governing the central pressure's time evolution was derived. Analysis of this equation reveals that its feasibility hinges on specific constraints regarding the constant $v_s$ and the initial central pressure. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a singularity arising in finite time is an inevitable consequence of these collapse conditions.

We employ the Iyer-Wald formalism to revisit the amendments proposed by Causino and others regarding the application of Smarr formulas and Kepler's laws to black holes possessing an arbitrary Lagrangian density derived from an arbitrary electromagnetic vector potential's field strength. Within this formalism, we demonstrate that the original corrections can be entirely reconstructed by incorporating specific additional terms into the Iyer-Wald scalar definition. Furthermore, although a comprehensive review of the first- and second-order contributions to both the Iyer-Wald scalar and surface form reveals significant deviations from standard formulations, we identify a consistent pattern. This underlying structure allows for the derivation of all necessary correction terms through the ampedification of the Iyer-W scalar using the Iyer-W formulation, thereby providing a unified approach to these modified dynamical laws.

Recent studies indicate that data located at the extremes of input sequences possess significantly less discriminative power compared to central information; however, most current models fail to effectively downweight these end-influences. Previous strategies for mitigating this issue include boundary masking and various pooling mechanisms aimed at reducing its impact. This paper instead proposes a novel computational approach designed to systematically lessen such interference throughout processing. Tests on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method consistently improves performance across the board. Furthermore, applied to the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets within a ResNet framework, the proposal achieves a significant accuracy boost over the standard (unmodified) network.

The Poincaré group functions as the symmetry framework for Poincaré-stable, free particles possessing positive mass squared. In contrast, vibrant mechanisms—also known as particle worldlines—embrace the full Poincaré manifold, encompassing zero (massless) states as well as those with negative mass squared. Within this comprehensive symmetry, particle mechanisms arise through specific symmetry-breaking processes. The term "negative mass squared" carries no adverse implications, as it signifies that certain modes are eliminated via mechanism-specific breaking, resulting in a physical subspace with strictly non-negative mass. The framework extends beyond the standard three spatial and one temporal dimension to accommodate these higher-dimensional particle worldlines. The study details an innovative mechanism wherein this higher-dimensional manifold decomposes via breaking into three distinct components: two corresponding to zero-mass squared (massless) states and one corresponding to a positive mass squared (massive) state. The positive mass squared component is identified as vibrant, meaning it corresponds to a localized particle mechanism situated within an auxiliary three-dimensional auxiliary space. The two massless vibrant components are interpreted as the two polarization modes of a single gravity particle. The mathematical structure of this mechanism relies on the vibrant symmetry-breaking inherent in the manifold's specific breaking pattern.

An upward planar drawing of a directed graph is one that remains planar while ensuring every edge follows the direction from lower to higher y-coordinates. For this visualization to exist, the graph's directed acyclic structure must align with a upward planar undirected spanning tree, where both drawings share the same underlying topology. This research introduces new parameterized algorithms for determining the combined layout of a directed acyclic graph and its upward planar spanning tree, with computational complexities of $O(2^k \cdot \text{poly}(n))$ for the kernelization step and $O((k+\log n)\cdot \text{poly}(n))$ for the solution phase, where $k$ represents the treewidth of the input graph.

This study introduces MemoNav, a new system for navigation that utilizes human memory. While prior research has explored how memory can enhance visual navigation, it has typically focused on remembering entire scenes rather than specific fragments. We propose that guiding navigation through fragmented memory fragments can be even more beneficial. We present an innovative technique to direct navigators using fragmented recollections. Evaluating this proposal on the prominent Visual Grounding Navigation (VGN) benchmark reveals the potential advantages ofse场景 (scene fragments) over full scene memory. However, utilizing fragment memories poses a significant challenge: determining which fragments a navigator should recall at any given moment. We address this by proposing MemoNav, which not only supports navigation using fragmented visual scenes but also decides which specific fragments to recall dynamically. To achieve this, we developed an innovative framework based on large language models (LLMs) to identify informative fragments. Although effective, this method requires substantial computational resources. To overcome this limitation, we developed a specialized memory module that enables vGNNN to learn to recall insightful fragments independently, without needing access to the LLM during operation. We have released our vGNNN code and model weights publicly to facilitate future research.

The advent of 5G has driven the deployment of extensive networks of small base stations, fueling the development of new technologies. This paper examines the evolution of the micro base station environment from 4G through projected 6G systems. It analyzes the history and evolution of small cells, outlines current research directions for next-generation small base stations, and investigates the convergence of machine learning with these networks. The work further explores the interplay between machine learning and artificial intelligence in shaping 6G, and details the evolution of machine learning itself to its next phase. Looking ahead, the study analyzes the potential evolution of machine learning for 6G and outlines the new challenges and research opportunities it presents.

Current research in the development of a unified theory connecting to the dynamics of hypergraphs is still in its early stages. This dissertation proposes a framework that extends dynamic frameworks used for graphs to include both univariate and multivariate occurrences within nets, all contained inside a hypergraph. This approach enables the application of existing theory—applied previously to mutual inductive networks, logical or biochemical systems, and neural architectures—to a singular, generalized hypergraphic structure. This method also facilitates introducing dynamics directly into the hyperedges themselves, distinct from the node-based focus of standard graph models within a hypergraph. Applying this framework, this work investigates path and cycle rules, flow networks, and both single-step and multi-step transformations occurring inside a hypergraph. This includes developing a theory of homomorphism mapping paths between structures while defining network equivalence through specific equivalence classes of flows within a hypergraph. This theory of flow equivalence partitions all flows into distinct categories defined by their structural relationship to a hypergraph, allowing for direct comparison. The operation of spatial dilation causes free scalar fields to transform into squeezed states characterized by the product of the field function with the spatial coordinate. This study examines how this transformation impacts the expansion of operators, specifically within the framework of 1+1 dimensional open bosonic string theory. The analysis reveals that the transformation leads to the factorization of the material part of the operator, leaving only spatial momentum-dependent factors in the non-spurious components. Furthermore, the computation of the expectation values for these squeezed states in the context of the light-cone gauge shows that the material momentum expectation values align with the simultaneous eigenstates of the operator $L_0$ and its momentum $P$.

Direct nuclear-decay experiments offer a unique perspective on the clusterization dynamics within light nuclei. This study presents the initial measurement of 16O decay into two nucleons and one alpha particle, with 8He emerging in an excitation state consistent with the Holet state. By utilizing a 16-MeV proton beam and applying the ionization time-proportion chamber technique, researchers achieved nearly background-free detection of the emitted electrons through their specific timing and topological signatures. The directly measured value of the matrix element, 16O(8He* + p + n) -> gamma(8He + p + n), aligns closely with theoretical predictions from ab initio methodologies. Furthermore, the precision of this observation enables the extraction of the 8He branching-ratio for radiative 16O decay, yielding \Gamma_\gamma = 0.11 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.03 \mu eV. These findings underscore the exceptional capabilities of direct-decay measurements in probing nuclear structure.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of oscillatory and tip-splitting phenomena in two-dimensional dynamic brittle fracture using finite-element simulations. The research examines how initial circular notches evolve into complex branching patterns in glass and polymer specimens, with a specific focus on oscillatory motion and tip division. The methodology involves a detailed map outlining the conditions required to generate these patterns, followed by a dimensionless parameter analysis to understand the influence of fracture velocity and initial notch dimensions. The findings indicate that while branching velocity is primarily dictated by the sample's inherent characteristic length, the oscillation amplitude is governed by the initial notch size. The discussion further explores the connection between these observed dynamics and the underlying physics of oscillatory and tip-dividing modes.

This paper examines reliable communication over a finite-state channel (FSC) with feedback. The standard model assumes the state information is tracked by a receiver-side automaton receiving a compressed state approximation via a bandwidth-limited feedback link. However, this work considers a state awareness scenario where the transmission strategy itself is regulated by an encoder-automaton constrained by identical bandwidth limitations. The analysis focuses on channels possessing the "strictly positive transition" property, ensuring every state state can transition to any other with non-zero probability. Under these conditions, this paper establishes that the information transmission capacity with state feedback equals the uncapacitated channel capacity, assuming the encoder state is noiselessly synced with the tracking state at the receiver. Additionally, for memoryless channels with additive states, sufficient conditions are derived to guarantee capacity attainment when feedback allows only one bit per step. These findings rely on a coupling of the Doss-Sztorzenberger theorem with the "Generalized Permutability Theorem" from Sztorzenberger.

The study examines the attractive Rashba Hubbard model, revealing a superfluid ground state characterized by zero angular momentum and topological properties, evidenced by a finite energy gap and Majorana zero modes in one-dimensional systems. Within the dynamical mean-field framework, we analyze the spectral and correlation properties of these states. It is shown that, unlike states with finite angular momentum, the singlet state lacks amplitude Goldstone modes but exhibits a pronounced dip in Goldstone-related correlations at low energies. Furthermore, we propose that the presence of long-standing quantum fluctuations in angular momentum is a critical prerequisite for forming this spin singlet superfluid state.

This paper details the submissions created for the Shared Task 9 at SemEval-2021, which focused on verifying facts within tables of scientific papers. Our task involved two subtasks: Subtask 1 required validating the correctness of individual fact statements concerning table data, while Subtask 2 aimed to locate the textual evidence supporting those validations. Subtask 1 was addressed using an ensemble of deep learning models trained on the provided dataset, whereas a diverse range of methods for evidence retrieval were tested for Subtask 2. Unfortunately, due to a lack of access to the training data set, participants could not train their models during the competition. Consequently, we executed our systems using the publicly available code and the large-scale pre-trained model BLOOM. The results presented reflect the outputs generated by this specific run under those constraints.

Intricate numbers, defined as $z = e^{i\theta}$ for real $\theta$, occupy a unique position in complex analysis. This discussion examines their properties within Quantum Physics. We demonstrate that the collection of intricate numbers constitutes a multiplicative subgroup of the unitary group $U(1)$ and a normal subgroup within the circle group. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the group of intricate numbers under multiplication and the group of real numbers under addition, specifically $\mathbb{R} \cong \{z \in \mathbb{C} | |z| = 1 \text{ and } z = e^{i\theta}, \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$. In the context of quantum mechanics, where the evolution operator is $e^{-iHt/\hbar}$, with $i$ as the imaginary unit, $t$ representing time, $\hbar$ the reduced Planck constant, and $H$ the Hamiltonian, we prove that if $\theta$ is restricted to rational values, the set of intricate numbers forms only a proper subgroup, whereas if $\theta$ is irrational, the set generates the entire circle group as a topologically generated structure.

A subset S of the vertex set V for a graph G=(V,E) is considered resolving if every vertex in V possesses a distinct metric representation relative to the set S. The metric dimension δ(G) corresponds to the minimal cardinality of such a resolving subset. This study introduces and examines the concept of shortening paths within a graph. A path is shortened by removing internal vertices that do not belong to the subset S. The shortened distance between vertices u and v, denoted as d_G^S(u,v), equals zero if the subset is empty; otherwise, it reflects the cardinality of the original path minus excluded vertices. A subset S is defined as shortening if every vertex in G has a unique shortened metric representation. The shortened metric dimension, denoted as sδ(G), is the lowest possible cardinality for this type of subset. This value naturally satisfies the inequality δ(G) ≥ sδ(G). This paper establishes several findings regarding graphs where the shortened dimension is strictly less than their standard metric dimension, specifically focusing on trees, unicyclic graphs, and cyclic graphs.

This study introduces two distinct mathematical formulations governing groundwater dynamics and water level changes due to non-capillary water transport in the porous medium. The first utilizes a mixed weak framework based on a specific set of strong formulation equations, while the second employs a non-divisorial weak framework based on an equivalent non-divisorial non-linear equation. For each formulation, existence and uniqueness of a weak solution are proven using the method of fixed points under assumptions of small data. In the scenario involving large data, both formulations utilize the pseudo-potential concept within an alternating-iterations algorithm to prove solution existence without assuming regularity on the water table. This approach adapts and extends methodologies previously established by S. Suli and M. C. Caltagirone for surface water-free conditions to the current context of extended groundwater and surface water zones.

This research investigates the potential of combining ozone and ultraviolet (UV) light to create a highly efficient system for removing sulfur dioxide (SO₂) from flue gas. The study utilizes a continuous flow, batch-wise photochemical reactor that integrates both UV light sources and an ozone injection mechanism. The reactor's design allows the generated ozone to penetrate the gas stream effectively, facilitating the oxidation of SO₂ into sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). The resulting acid is subsequently trapped in an aqueous ammonia scrubber, converting it into ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄), a valuable fertilizer. The experimental results indicate that this combined ozone-UV approach offers a promising pathway for creating a compact, energy-efficient method for desulfurizing flue gases while simultaneously producing high-value fertilizers.

Although general-purpose languages like C++ and SystemC support the development of both neural networks and individual hardware components, they fall short in providing comprehensive tooling for the integration and co-simulation of these heterogeneous elements. Additionally, the unique asynchronous nature of neuromorphic networks requires specific simulation techniques distinct from those used on conventional sequential circuits. This paper introduces VNCAB, a systemic framework built upon SystemC designed to streamline the prototyping of large-scale neuromorphic systems. By integrating pre-existing IP modules for network algorithms with specialized support for internal events, external stimuli, and notifications, VNCAB facilitates efficient co-design. The inclusion of dual scheduling mechanisms enables the network to adapt dynamically to varying time scales, ensuring accurate behavior across different granularities.

We introduce Indecision Forests, a novel machine learning architecture designed to handle ambiguity in regression tasks by deliberately refraining from selecting optimal splits during the growth of decision trees. This approach is implemented via a modified version of the CART algorithm that selects a subset of top-performing splits rather than just the single best one at each step. To train these models, we developed an optimization framework based on multi-objective learning to balance predictive accuracy with the diversity of potential splits. We evaluated Indecision Forests against standard models on both synthetic and real-world datasets, confirming their superior ability to capture complex nonlinear patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the generated trees can support explainable AI by offering multiple, justified decisions that align with human reasoning under uncertainty.

Disability Time Warping (DTW) serves as a highly effective method for measuring the resemblance between time-sequential data; however, the complexity of standard $m$-dimensional time series with length $N$ scales quadratically, or $O(N^2)$, rendering a direct comparison between two such series computationally prohibitive. Recently, a variant known as **pruned DTW** has emerged, capable of reducing the complexity of calculating single series to $O(N \lambda^2)$, where $\lambda$ is a length factor that is significantly smaller than $N$. This efficiency allows for significantly faster processing. This paper introduces **Pruned $\lambda$-TW**, a novel distance metric calculated in $O(N \lambda^2)$ time, which is a specialized, faster version of pruned DTW. Additionally, we present **early discarding**, a straightforward yet powerful strategy to reduce the computational complexity of $m$-dimensional time series comparisons from $O(N \lambda^2)$ to $O(N \lambda^2)$ by allowing for the early termination of comparisons. We also describe **Pruned TW-SimSearch**, an algorithm that leverages the pruned TW distance to conduct similarity searches. This approach combines the early discarding technique with an index structure to accelerate search operations. Testing represents a vital component of the software development lifecycle, and the ability to design and execute tests is a core competency for professional software engineers. Despite its significance, the prevalence of testing practices within industry remains surprisingly low. To investigate whether instructional strategies could enhance testing awareness within a industrial context, this study compared two teaching methodologies: an inquiry-based, concept-focused system and a traditional approach providing detailed feedback. Empirical data gathered from 122 undergraduate students indicated that while both methods yielded no significant difference in actual testing tasks or self-perceived competence, the inquiry-based, conceptual strategy significantly boosted students' testing awareness more effectively than conventional instruction with specific technical feedback.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at high-precision, black-box tasks like medical image diagnosis, their lack of transparency poses risks in critical fields due to safety concerns. Conversely, Constraint-based Inductive Logic Programming (CILP) offers its own opaque limitations by generating models filled with complex, hard-to-interpret constraints. This study introduces a hybrid model that leverages the strengths of both DNNs and CILP to create human-understandable explanations. The approach begins by using a DNN to identify input errors, which are then incorporated into soft constraints within a CILP framework. This generates initial logic rules for clarifications that are refined through iterative retraining. Ruled representations are formatted into natural language to generate detailed explanations. Testing on the complex numerical task of TIGER diagonal recognition confirmed that this iteration effectively produces accurate rule-based clarifications with minimal reliance on the initial DNN component.

Recently, the in-depth analysis of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) has revealed that they function as low-pass filters, which inherently limit their capacity to generalize due to over-smoothing. Although several studies have recently addressed these inherent constraints, the specific mechanism through which the low-pass characteristic causes distinct failure modes, known as over-blurring, remains unclear. In this work, we investigate this over-blurring phenomenon by introducing an analytical framework that elucidates how the inherent filtering properties of GCNs lead to distinct degradation patterns. Specifically, we derive a metric to quantify the probability of these failures, enabling the prediction of their occurrence based on input graph structures. Our experimental results, conducted across various scenarios, validate the effectiveness of this new over-blurring measure. Furthermore, building on these insights, we introduce a novel architecture designed to mitigate over-blurring while preserving the advantages of message-passing graph convolutions.

In this paper, we investigate spaces equipped with "stockings," representing a novel extension of topological groups. This framework allows for a new approach to analyzing uniform structures on X through the lens of uniform spaces defined on X×X. We demonstrate that spaces with stockings form a category where colimits exist and are formulated as extended versions of standard topological groups. Furthermore, we apply this method to characterize uniform spaces compatible with quadratic expansions and those supporting vectorization.

Controlling the growth of high-quality, crystalline thin films is essential for advancing both fundamental research and technological applications. A primary factor influencing this process is the epitaxial alignment between the film and substrate, which occurs through a combination of lattice-matching (van der Waals), pinhole formation, and elastic deformation effects. While this interaction typically results in a mosaic of strained domains and epitaxial misalignment, recent studies suggest that growth conditions can be tuned to regulate the balance among these contributing mechanisms. This work examines the evolution of Heusler layer structures as a function of growth temperature by analyzing their composition, out-of-plane lattice parameters, in-plane domain orientation, and strain levels. Specifically, it focuses on the $X_{1-}Y$ interface, where $X$ represents the (0001)-oriented aluminum-doped graphene on (0001)-oriented sapphire substrate and $Y$ denotes the (001)-oriented body-centered cubic (BCC) Heusler alloy. By combining experimental data with first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the study establishes a comprehensive picture of film evolution and offers a predictive model for future material-substrate pairings.

We establish the weak consistency and asymptotic normality of these models. The Hubble Space Telescope's inability to resolve the multiple images of the lensed quasar ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, located within the nearby galaxy cluster Act-Cl J0102$-$4915 (a common misspelling is Act-Cl J0102$-$4915), has hindered efforts to characterize the foreground lens. However, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has now successfully resolved these multipel images of the quasar, revealing a new cosmological red supergiant (RSG) in the foreground. In this work, we present a new lens model for ACT-Cl J0102$-$4915, incorporating the quasar and a sample of 128 R/IR-excess sources as lensed galaxies. We also identify a previously unknown R/IR-excess source, designated R/IR-excess source 129, as a new lensed galaxy. Using this refined model, we determine that the quasar's redshift is $z=1.97$ and that the lensed galaxy at ACT-Cl J0102$-$4915 has a red supergiant at a redshift of $z=10.00$. This discovery marks the most distant red supergiant known to date.

This study examines a market environment comprising multiple network operators and content providers, focusing on how they share profits and make strategic decisions. Specifically, it investigates the interdependence between profit-sharing mechanisms and the strategic choices content providers make regarding which networks to utilize and the data volume transmitted. To address this, the authors develop a multi-level game model that begins with network operators defining their revenue-sharing terms. Subsequently, content providers strategize based on these agreements to select networks and determine service levels. Finally, the work analyzes the impact of varying profit-sharing terms on the content distribution strategies offered by those providers.

$\alpha$-attractor models have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their theoretical elegance and promising cosmological predictions. This work provides a comprehensive review of $\alpha$-attractor theory, unifying the various mathematical frameworks offered by different researchers and illustrating the relationships between them. Additionally, we explore the forecasting capabilities of these models, specifically through the lens of inflationary parameters and post-inflationary observables derived from primordial gravitational waves. By analyzing the distinct predictions of each model framework, we highlight their unique signatures within the space of forecastable quantities.

This paper presents a novel perspective on the Kereki-Malpiedi theorem by introducing a continuous deformation. Kerékjártó's original result establishes a continuity relationship between the space of quasi-Fuchsian structures in a given Fuchsian conjugacy class and that of the corresponding Fuchsian surface. In contrast, our approach maps these objects to the boundary of the associated quasi-Fuchsian structure. We demonstrate that there exists a deformation keeping the underlying Fuchsian surface invariant while producing every quasi-Fuchsian structure within its conjugacy class. This finding constitutes an adaptation and extension of an existing strategy by M. Kapovich.

This study investigates the dispersion of portfolio yields within a general framework that permits yields to be arbitrary random variables, potentially lacking well-defined moments, and remains valid even under weak regularity conditions regarding the joint distribution of yields and initial portfolio weights. The principal finding establishes that the dispersion of final portfolio values is governed by the yield variance only as a secondary factor; instead, mean yield dispersion is driven overwhelmingly by how mean yields correlate with initial portfolio weights. The provided derivation offers closed-form solutions for both the variance contribution from weights and the secondary variance yield terms, alongside the complete joint distribution of final values. The findings have significant practical utility, as the approach enables precise calculations of yield dispersion for any conceivable set of yields, a capability further demonstrated through multiple examples in the paper.

Heart sound categorization is essential for cardiac disease detection and monitoring. While cardiac interference is a significant factor, existing research has not fully addressed its impact on categorization systems. To mitigate these interference effects, we introduced a new methodology utilizing Additive Noise Removal (ARR) to subtract interference directly from the signal, alongside a network architecture employing asymmetric convolutional deformation to handle heart sound data. The study employed the CNN model PhyonNet, which uses asymmetric dilation for the deconvolved signal outputs from ARR. The proposed methodology was validated using two datasets: the public collection and the newly recorded set. The results demonstrate that this approach outperforms a baseline configuration without preprocessing, achieving superior classification accuracy.

In our study, we calculated upper bounds for the two specified beyond-Standard-Model (BSM) operators—$ \mathcal{O}_{\phi q}^{(1)} $ and $ \mathatomic parity violation in the electroweak sector—by leveraging a specific BSM model framework that links the atomic scale to high-scale physics through matching. This methodology yielded significantly different outcomes compared to the calculations by the JHEP1708 article, which utilized matching within a general, scheme-dependent effective field theory (EFT) to derive these limits. The core reason for this discrepancy lies in the lack of specification regarding renormalization scale and scheme choices in their approach, rendering their derived bounds not only highly scale and scheme dependent but also generally less restrictive. Because their procedure ties the atomic scale to both high-scale physics and the specific technical definition of their general EFT, their results fail to isolate the true physical constraints of new physics. Consequently, our findings are physically determined by the actual scale of the new phenomena and represent limits that are robust against variations in renormalization scale and scheme.

This study examines how social structures influence climate change, with a specific focus on family configurations, marriage, and childbearing patterns. Using unique register data from Denmark, the authors track individual births, marriages, and separations across the late 20th and early 21st centuries. While acknowledging that shifts in these structures cannot alone account for declining fertility rates, the analysis demonstrates that individuals within married households are markedly more prone to marrying again upon separation and exhibit lower fertility compared to those remaining single. Consequently, the authors argue that declining importance of traditional family forms may have contributed to fertility decline by facilitating later first marriages and first unions, thereby delaying childbearing.

This paper presents a comprehensive study of weighted $l^p$ spaces, denoted as $\mathcal{H}^p_\alpha$, consisting of all bounded discrete transforms that are invertible for fractional transforms with $\alpha > 0$ and $1 < p < \infty$. The analysis establishes key operator theory results, including characterizing the adjoints of key operators like shift, projection, and dilation, as well as identifying when specific operators like projection and dilation are positive. The authors also determine the exact bounds for the norms of projection and dilation.

This study involves participants bidding on hundreds of items in repeated second-price auctions to observe their responses to both honest and deceptive auctions featuring fake prices. The primary findings indicate that honesty rates drop significantly when auctions are falsified, yet most participants continue to report truthfully even after discovering the deception. Furthermore, the trust provided by an initial honest experience boosts honesty in subsequent auctions, while witnessing fraud leads participants to be more likely to cheat later on. However, prior trust does not influence the magnitude of future bids or bid variability. These results suggest that while fraud diminishes the probability of honesty, it does not necessarily cause individuals to fully abandon their ethical standards.

We investigate the evolution of locally rotationally symmetric (LRS) locally anisotropic homogeneous cosmological models within the Bianchi-I framework using $f(Q)$-gravity, an extension of the teleparallel equivalent of general relativity based on the non-metricity scalar $Q$. The study derives the specific form of the function $f(Q)$ required to achieve the early isotropization of the universe. It is demonstrated that the proposed gravity model successfully induces this isotropization for both the perfect fluid case as well as when a scalar field with appropriate parameters drives the expansion.

Neural networks have become a prominent tool for generating visual art, yet they often produce results that lack variety and are overly similar to their training data. This paper introduces "Delight," an approach leveraging aesthetic guidelines to enhance the diversity of AI-generated artwork. Delight functions by evaluating generated pieces against specific criteria, such as harmony, and employs back-propagation through the classifier to perform targeted image editing. This process involves pushing a representation away from an "unpleasant" state in feature space, thereby maximizing the desired aesthetic quality. Rather than simply making artwork more beautiful, this method of over-optimizing the opposite quality effectively heightens the specific trait, resulting in more engaging and delightful pieces. Experiments on the TestArt dataset demonstrate enhancements in style variety without compromising the image's overall appearance while also showing increased diversity in artistic rendering.

Recent LHCb analyses have revealed irregularities in the flavor physics parameters $\mathcal{B}$ and $K$, denoted as the $b$-anomaly and the strangequark anomaly, respectively. This work interprets these discrepancies as evidence for a composite nature in down-type interactions, specifically through the introduction of color-octet scalar and fermion fields that mediate four-fermion interactions between down-type and up-type quarks. This theoretical framework simultaneously addresses the $b$-anomaly and the strangequark anomaly, while also imposing significant constraints on the new particles' masses and coupling parameters. Furthermore, we explore the connection between this compositeness and the electroweak sector, specifically focusing on the composition of $W$ and $Z$ bosons arising from scalar fermion loops, which can resolve the anomaly in vector boson production observed in the Tevatron.

Knowledge-seeking Question Answering (KSQA)—a recently introduced paradigm focused on forming answers to information-seeking inquiries by utilizing entire documents—has prompted continued research into effective KSQA system strategies. This study presents the first public dataset tailored for evaluating knowledge-seeking QP answering, featuring 2,385 such queries and 2,080 corresponding responses derived from scholarly articles across five academic disciplines. Complementing the data are additional auxiliary materials, including the queries themselves rephrased and human-identified relevant passage segments. Constructed via automated extraction from papers and subsequent manual refinement, our corpus is grounded in real-world academic instances of knowledge-seeking behavior. Recognizing the manual annotation involved, we propose this resource will facilitate and enhance future research within the KSQA field.

This study examines the rapidity of core-collapse supernovae, specifically analyzing the timescales of neutrally mediated nuclear processes in the early post-bounce phase. Using data from a recent 3D simulation, this work evaluates the rapidity of collapse based on the time required for these reactions to reach equilibrium. We identify that the neutrally mediated nuclear processes' rate of occurrence is primarily dictated by the density and temperature of the environment, as well as the energy spectrum of emitted particles. Additionally, we observe that the early dynamics are heavily influenced by the initial state of the proto-neutron star, particularly its size and thermal evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that magnetic fields can significantly alter these timescales, potentially accelerating the process by orders of magnitude in specific regions. These findings provide valuable insights into the underlying physics governing rapid core-collapse supernovae, with potential implications for multi-messenger astronomy and the synthesis of heavy elements.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, with no current biological markers available for diagnosis. Machine learning models trained on resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) have shown promise in classifying ADHD patients, though these approaches typically analyze the entire brain without pinpointing specific regions driving the classification. This study introduces a novel framework that identifies crucial areas contributing to ADHD classification using deep learning on rs-fMRI data. The process involves extracting features from the entire scan, performing gradient-based backpropagation to calculate feature importance, and subsequently reconstructing high-level representations using only the most significant vascular regions. Results from a dataset of 212 participants (107 with ADHD, 105 controls) revealed that the proposed method achieved comparable accuracy to full-brain models. Furthermore, this region-specific approach yielded superior performance when evaluated under conditions of data scarcity.

We introduce epidemic SISI model, distinguishing itself by allowing susceptible individuals to be infected only within a restricted, fixed duration. By employing a distinct, fixed timeframe for infection, we account for the fact that susceptibility is time-limited. This paper presents a stochastic SISI framework on Erdős–Rényi graphs to examine the dynamics of this process during the early phase of an epidemic, when only a small number of individuals are infected. This approach complements existing continuous epidemic models, which assume that susceptibility persists indefinitely until infection. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the epidemic cannot take root among these transiently susceptible individuals. Furthermore, assuming the process does spread, we establish convergence results showing that the total ultimately infected count converges, in distribution, during the early stages of an epidemic.

Acronyms are ubiquitous in technical documentation, research papers, and social media, yet they often pose significant barriers for non-native speakers, visually impaired users, and individuals unaware of their meanings. To address this challenge, we introduce MadDog, a web-based platform designed to allow users to acquire acronym-related knowledge simply by submitting any undefined term. Our system leverages a hybrid approach that integrates data-driven techniques with a cloud-based dictionary to offer comprehensive explanations, effectively combining statistical efficiency with the robustness of knowledge representation through semantic networks. To validate our methodology and demonstrate the system's functionality, we present a real-world case study featuring the analysis of the #COVID19 hashtag on Twitter.

This study introduces a novel strategy for directional control of heat and power in mesoscale systems, grounded in the unique properties of Quantum Hall (QH) edge states. By employing a QH bar detector operating as a dual-source, two-terminal thermoelectric device, we utilize a third source gate to selectively activate either a single edge state or allow the coexistence of multiple states. Our analysis reveals that within this configuration, the switchable nature of theQH modes generates a modulated Seebeck coefficient and resistance, giving rise to distinct phenomena such as fine structure in open-circuit voltage, oscillating behavior in short-circuit current, and non-linear power output. Notably, we observe a peak in power density when only one mode is permitted, whereas prohibiting their simultaneous presence triggers "thermoelectric toggling." This mechanism ensures that a system heated on both sides can still produce electricity, effectively resolving a critical limitation inherent in conventional generators. Furthermore, the identified effects facilitate the design of compact, high-efficiency heat diodes and rectors, establishing a fresh avenue for thermal management in quantum-based electronic architectures.

Deletion errors are prevalent in DNA storage and can severely disrupt downstream processing if unaddressed. Existing solutions typically employ forward error correction (FEC) bits to recover a limited number of deletion positions; however, these methods often fail to utilize specific characteristics inherent to the DNA data structure. This paper introduces a new FEC-assisted framework leveraging indexing mechanisms to effectively mitigate multiple deletion mistakes. This approach exploits two key features: (1) the mutual uniqueness of indexing entries and (2) the hierarchical organization of the index. First, we present a general algorithm that combines the uniqueness property with FEC to resolve multiple deletions. Subsequently, we develop updates that maintain this hierarchical format within the index. Together, these contributions as a suite of codes that adapt DNA's structural properties, offering enhanced resilience against widespread deletion bursts. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior resilience against extensive deletion events, requires fewer FEC bits than current FEC-assisted solutions, and facilitates efficient storage and retrieval during index modifications.

Topological insulators and semimetals are defined by protected nodal lines within their energy spectra. When these lines curve or exhibit lines of quadratic touching, they can be characterized by surface charges known as nodal line charges. This study offers a thorough analysis of these non-trivial topological structures, detailing their properties and recent realizations using light and other systems. We define a precise topological charge for a line by calculating the self-intersection number of their corresponding nodal surface, reinterpreting this surface charge as the magnetic flux from a gauge field acting on a hypothetical fermion charged under the same gauge. Using photonic setups, this charge is demonstrated through the magnetic-like fields themselves. Furthermore, we outline strategies for modifying the three-dimensional shape of the associated nodal surfaces by manipulating the material's topology.

Previous studies have utilized various methodologies to determine the propagation speed of traveling waves in excitable media, relying on different underlying assumptions. In this study, we apply a distinct approach to estimate propagation velocities by integrating the spatio-temporal evolution of wave pacemakers with that of wavefronts. This method is demonstrated using the well-known Barkley model, where the calculated speed aligns closely with both numerical simulations and experimental observations. Furthermore, this technique is viable for other models characterized by their simple structure.

Entropic quantities are essential for analyzing quantum information systems. This paper presents two novel, efficient quantum algorithms that approximate entropy and conditional entropy for arbitrary distributions of pure states on a fixed space. One of these methods operates with query complexity $O(\max\{1,\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)(\log n+n\log(1/\epsilon)/\epsilon^2)\}$, where $n$ is the local Hilbert dimension, while the other offers an alternative trade-off between different resources. We demonstrate that these algorithms are nearly optimal by establishing a lower bound of $O(\max\{1,\epsilon^{-2}\log(nn/\epsilon^2)\log(1/\delta)\})$. Additionally, the results extend to scenarios where only limited access to the corresponding unitary operators is available.

This document outlines the storage duration for AI-related data within AWS R5 instances and examines cloud environment strategies to minimize costs associated with data processing. Additionally, it introduces MLOps and L.Ops frameworks and analyzes the technical components of artificial intelligence workflow management.

This study addresses ICD coding using a semi-supervised deep learning framework. The design of our framework is grounded in the hypothesis that ICD codes exhibit significant local regularity; specifically, symptoms or diseases sharing similar characteristics tend to converge within the same latent latent space. To validate this, we developed a semi-supervised autoencoder, where the encoder extracts local features and the corresponding decoder ensures codes mapping to相近 traits remain proximate in latent space. To address data scarcity, we employ data augmentation to synthetically expand training sets. Additionally, we apply data consistency principles to maintain ICD classification integrity across iteratively augmented data. Evaluated on the ICD-9 dataset, our method surpasses existing benchmarks, achieving precision of 0.803, recall of 0.790, and an F1 score of 0.796.

Cohen-Macaulay (CM) rings and CM-free modules are well-established within commutative algebra, whereas the concept of nearly CM was recently proposed. This paper provides new findings and numerous examples concerning the properties of nearly CM monomial ideals.

We present the results of a systematic investigation into celestial anomalies observed in the 2018 KMTNet celestial survey, which covered 2.5% of the sky across the Milky Way bulge and disk. This study defines a total of 23 distinct categories of anomalies, organized into 13 groups based on their visual characteristics and 13 further classified by their underlying causes. For each type, we detail the total count of occurrences, the proportion attributed to specific causes, and the associated detection methods. To comprehensively address every identified category, we compiled a total sample size of 23. This work serves as a critical reference for the identification and management of various anomalous signals in future exoplanet transit anomaly observations.

This paper introduces a novel, rapid technique for generating shadow images within visual inference frameworks. We find that standard gradient-based optimization struggles to resolve opaque occlusions effectively, resulting in poor OOQ generalization for these issues. Although prior methods mitigate opacity by blending multiple observations, they incur substantial computational delays. We propose a solution that leverages neural network-derived contact maps and differentiable shadow synthesis to process divergences among images where opaque bodies are partially visible. This approach enables the network to clarify ambiguous visual signals, improving general capability on tasks involving shadows. The algorithm integrates an innovative, learnable differential shadow module that can be trained end-to-end alongside the core network. We have validated this methodology across two distinct visual inference domains, and the outcomes demonstrate that it surpasses existing techniques in both speed and out-of-sample performance.

This study introduces a new statistical approach for deriving origin-destination (OD) pairs from daily traffic snapshots, focusing on the divergence between true OD matrices and those estimated via traffic counts. The authors present two upper bounds on this matrix discrepancy: the first applies specifically to fully congested networks, while the second is universal. Leveraging these bounds, the authors propose an estimator aimed at minimizing the estimated errors, demonstrating through both numerical and real-world experiments that this method achieves superior accuracy compared to existing solutions.

Recent studies have revealed that random arrays of autonomous oscillators, subject to arbitrary long-range interactions governed by a time-varying kernel with significant temporal memory, can exhibit striking inhomogeneous synchronous behavior. This phenomenon arises in systems spanning from quantum to biological scales and involves two distinct synchronization modes: one where oscillation frequencies are desynchronized but amplitudes align, and another where both amplitudes and frequencies synchronize. We extend this framework to non-autonomous systems influenced by stochastic noise and time-dependent forcing, adapting the previously identified amplitude-only and frequency-amplitude-only synchronization concepts to these newer contexts. Specifically, we investigate how the coupling kernel shapes synchronous patterns in arrays composed of diverse oscillators that differ in their intrinsic frequencies, amplitudes, or environmental responses. Ultimately, we demonstrate that these synchronized states serve as robust foundations for organizing collective activity in complex networks.

Aldous-Broder and Wilson's algorithms are renowned for producing uniform spanning trees via random walks, yet a direct mapping between the two was previously elusive. This paper presents a theoretical algorithm that generates USTs by integrating both methods. The core innovation is a two-phase structure, where the initial phase simulates a synchronous, parallel execution of a single, generalized random walk, while the second phase simulates specific conjugations based on the trajectory of that walk. The first phase is shown to be statistically equivalent to a coordinated sequence of independent Wilson algorithms, and the second phase establishes the necessary equivalence to a simultaneous, parallel execution of $N$ independent Wilson algorithms. This structural identity allows us to prove that the outputs of the two algorithms are identical. Furthermore, the authors provide an upper bound estimate for the number of walk steps required in the first phase to match the logarithmic growth rate found in the standard Wilson algorithm. Although the conversion between sheet music, musical audio, and lyrics is a practical necessity, current methods rely on isolated models because the large volumes of paired data required for such a task do not exist in a unified format. To address this, we introduce the **MusicTM-Dataset**, which is publicly available and focused on the multimodal representation of sheet music, audio, and textual lyrics. Leveraging this resource, we developed a unified cross-modal representation model that enhances existing methods. We also created the **MusicTM-Dataset** by applying advanced neural network techniques to process the sheets, audio, and lyrics simultaneously. We also introduced a unified cross-modal modeling framework that allows us to extract more information from the sheets, audio, and lyrics simultaneously.

This study explores how pre-trained embedding models, such as Word2Vec and GloVe, can be applied to visualize and analyze ontologies. The proposed methodology involves generating visual representations directly from pre-existing vector data, utilizing an algorithm that constructs a graph structure by identifying significant word associations within the embedded sets. This approach leverages the prepared distance metrics between concepts to establish network links, offering a fresh perspective on structural analysis by combining static embeddings with graph-based exploration tools like Ontodia and Wikidata.

The presence of an intensity-dependent modulation of the nonlinear coefficient and the nonlinear frequency shift is a characteristic feature of many optical systems. Within this context, we examine the mathematical framework to analyze the stability of dark solitaries. Our findings indicate that incorporating a variable dispersion range expands the parameter region for stable solitaries compared to the constant dispersion model. Additionally, we identify new mechanisms capable of generating and controlling the acceleration of these entities.

Interpreting extensive and intricate datasets remains a significant challenge, prompting researchers to explore various interactive methods for visual analysis. However, existing systems typically address only narrow, specific tasks, necessitating adaptable and extensible platforms that allow analysts to deploy diverse interventions across diverse VLANA. To this end, we introduce Lotse, an open framework enabling the visualization of interactive visual elements within any visual analytics context. Furthermore, we expand Lotce by proposing Functional Assistance (FUNA), a strategy for introducing the visual instructions within it. We detail Lotce's design and implementation, demonstrating its utility by adapting two distinct active learning models—covering both dataset and schema learning—to the framework. Our contributions include an empirical assessment of Lotce through its release on Maven Central, thereby establishing a comprehensive software library accessible to other researchers for alternative applications.

Optimizing stellarators for improved confinement and symmetry necessitates adjusting the shapes of their modular coils, an iterative process that currently relies on human expertise alongside computational tools. This study introduces a capability within the OpenFOAM-based stellarator coil enhancement (SCE) software to support various coil configurations. Initially, an axisymmetric example is examined to validate the method's efficacy in enhancing stellarator geometry across different modular setups, demonstrating its utility in managing complex magnetic configurations.

A non-invasive experimental technique utilizing MRI is applied to visualize temperature variations in an air-water vapor-nonaqueous solvent vapor mixture flowing through a packed bed. High-resolution, real-time temperature distributions are achieved by monitoring the changes in the proton spin relaxation rates of the stationary particles caused by solvent vapors. This MRI-based approach offers significant advantages over traditional point-based thermocouples, providing comprehensive spatial and temporal thermal profiles within the bed. Additionally, the experimental data are compared against simulations based on a porous media model to validate their consistency.

This study investigates the self-organization of self-assembling biomolecular units that form aggregates with open ends, where interaction strength depends on temperature and the chemical state of the monomer. These monomers consist of simple square blocks featuring specific functional end-groups. Through a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and a coarse-grained model, the research explores the self-assembly of these blocks into two distinct aggregate structures: one composed of vertically aligned blocks and another of horizontally aligned blocks. The analysis reveals that these two types of aggregates act as complementary components of a single supramolecular assembly, which is generated through the end-to-end interaction of vertically arranged clusters. This higher-order organization drives the self-sorting of monomers based on their functional state and enables the storage and release of chemical energy through inter-aggregate interactions that convert chemical differences into mechanical work.

This study examines the evolution of sunspot groups and magnetic disturbances during solar eruptions, utilizing data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) for Active Region (AR) 11429, which exhibited a $\Delta$-shaped dominant magnetic polarity. The region was monitored from October 13 to October 20, 2013, capturing the development of its leading spot and the subsequent flare events triggered by magnetic reconnection. The initial sunspot emerged on October 13 with a width of 13.8 Mm and a length of 18.2 Mm. By October 15, a secondary spot appeared adjacent to the primary one, narrowing the separation between them. The investigation identifies the primary sunspot as a composite structure formed by merging smaller spots and notes that the space between the composite elements housed a magnetic neutral line. The paper concludes that the reconnection of magnetic field lines across this internal neutral line induced the rotational motion of the leading spot and generated the flares observed on October 15 and October 16.

The study explores the stability of the principle b under the condition that an unstable model satisfies T_b. This hypothesis N is independent from pr and posits that every non-trivial cardinal is b-primal. Furthermore, we provide specific examples of theories where the principle N is equivalent to the condition b itself, including the theory of the natural numbers equipped with both ordering and addition.

Accurate predictions of cardiac mechanics rely on robust numerical methods, which in turn demand efficient solvers for large sparse systems of equations arising from discretization. This research introduces a novel comparison of various preconditioners for these specific linear problems, extending existing work by employing the hypre Multilevel Infinitesimal Boundary condition (MLBIC) framework alongside other preconditioners using Scalable Library for Linear Algebra Subprograms (SLALIB). Synthesized results reveal that when paired with the Krylov subspace solver BiCGSTAB, MLBiLBi consistently outperforms competing approaches by significantly reducing computation times. Moreover, this approach delivers superior solution accuracy and demonstrates scalable solutions.

Social tagging systems allow users to collaboratively label and share resources, offering valuable insights into collective knowledge discovery. This paper investigates the temporal patterns of collaborative activity within OpenCyberplace, an Indonesian social tagging system. Our analysis reveals that both individual user contributions and collaboration frequencies exhibit a highly intermittent distribution, characterized by brief active bursts followed by prolonged quiet intervals. Interestingly, both individual activity levels and collaboration rates are positively correlated with one another. Additionally, we examined several attributes of shared resources and their impact on usage patterns over time. Findings indicate that attributes associated with richer interest exchange—specifically detailed descriptions and rich metadata—strongly correlate with more sustained temporal adoption. In contrast, resource attributes linked to utility, such as high ratings and abundant views, drive usage that is more burst-oriented. These results highlight how different resource qualities serve distinct functions: attributes promoting interest encourage long-term engagement, whereas those promoting utility foster short-term, intense use.

The evolution of 5G wireless networks demands new technologies to connect all devices, a challenge met by Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB). First defined in 3GPP Release 17, iAB allows small IAx base stations to utilize remaining 3Ax base station resources, enabling simultaneous access and backhaul links over a shared medium. This article outlines the fundamental principles of Integrated Access and Backhaul, examines the major challenges and possible remedies, and highlights key differences between legacy and new architectures. We also explore the primary technical and deployment hurdles that could delay or prevent the widespread adoption of mobile IAx in future cellular systems.

The Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) task involves adjusting algorithm configuration variables to enhance performance. This paper examines how to establish values for the Hyperparameter of the Evolutionary Algorithm (AEA) that improve the performance of the One-Objective Global Optimization Algorithm (OGOA). The approach employs the Morris L-OFT method to evaluate interactions among hyperparameters and the Sobol' method to quantify their individual significance. The results demonstrate that the Computation of the Fitness Function (CFF) and the Competition Strength (CS) are the most critical independent AEA parameters, with the tournament size (TS) also being highly significant; furthermore, these three exhibit substantial interactions with one another. The study reveals that the top-performing OAG configurations are C=10, C=20, and T=20, while the optimal combination for OAG is C=10, C=20, and T=20.

Hydrodynamic analogues of quantum mechanics offer intuitive frameworks for deriving Schrödinger's equation. In this paper, we demonstrate that these analog systems can be extended to scenarios involving mesons and hadrons as well as scenarios involving changes in size and the transition from non-relativistic to relativistic regimes. Specifically, we derive the non-relativistic wave equations for both cases and introduce corresponding relativistic variants. Notably, these derived wave equations align with those proposed independently by Makhlin and colleagues. Finally, we examine several properties of the wave functions produced; these include inherent probability current conservation, the relationship between probability density and current, and the calculation of expectation values for both energy and position.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) methods are primarily validated using static, isolated, and narrowly defined benchmarks, which often leads to strategies that merely memorize specific tasks or produces results that lack generativity. Consequently, these methods struggle to adapt to evolving, unpredictable, and progressively difficult environments. To rectify this flaw, we introduce L2Explorer, a comprehensive ecosystem designed to facilitate the evaluation of RL approaches for progressive skill acquisition within continuously changing conditions. Within this framework, agents confront a variety of tasks that evolve over time, demanding the development of transferable strategies capable of handling any potential progression path. We detail the architectural design and generation methodology of our task universe, which is hosted at a publicly accessible website. This platform also includes baseline algorithms and extensive experimental data to support future research. We introduce this L2Explorer framework to promote more robust and generalizable solutions for learning skills under dynamic conditions.

For over a decade, Liger (Imaging and Spectroscopy at Keck Observatory) has operated as a facility for imaging and spectroscopy. As a software-defined system, it offers significant flexibility to users, researchers, and the operations team. This work details Liger's progress in software development, specifically the data processing infrastructure and its connections to other software. Additionally, it addresses file formats, the Keck Observatory Data System (KODIS), and the integration points with external modules, including the image display tool Kodex and the data reduction package drliger.
