The proposed hadron spectrometer aims to detect charged particles within energy ranges of 2 to 250 GeV, leveraging proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. Leveraging its compact dimensions, the instrument is well-suited for installation in both surface and underground environments. Radiation-hardened silicon pixel and strip detectors will map the trajectories of charged particles, while an array of dense scintillator tiles will measure their energy loss. Additionally, forward-chicane magnetic fields will enable momentum determination through curvature analysis, and Cherenkov light detection will identify particle identities up to approximately 250 GeV/c$^2$. Radiative correction effects will be managed through precise timing, enabling the system to achieve comprehensive particle identification across the full 2–250 GeV energy spectrum.

This study introduces a novel orientation convolutional architecture designed to enhance pattern recognition in images. Unlike standard networks that employ sequential processing, this framework utilizes two parallel streams working side by side. The first network analyzes images with the usual forward progression, while the second inverts image orientations at every convolutional layer. By merging the outputs of both models, the system effectively amplifies the feature representations learned. Experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets reveal that this approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieves an accuracy of 89.9% on CIFAR-10 and 74.6% on CIFAR-100, while the computation remains efficient with only a minor increase in memory requirements.

Point cloud data, which captures 3D spatial distributions, is widely used in applications like medical imaging and autonomous driving. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become the standard for processing point clouds by constructing graphs based on point pair distances, they often fail on sparse or irregular clouds because k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) graph generation creates disconnected components. This paper introduces P-GCNet, a novel framework designed specifically to handle such challenging scenarios. Our approach utilizes a dual-graph strategy that builds two complementary graphs via k-Nearest and l-Furthest neighbors to effectively cover fragmented parts of irregular clouds. Furthermore, a new distance metric is introduced to more accurately model relationships within these complex structures. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that P-GCNet significantly outperforms existing methods in handling sparse and irregular point clouds, offering a robust solution for real-world medical applications.

While current Trojans in deep learning primarily rely on modifying semantics to create effective and stealthy injections, this paper introduces a novel, host-dependent model that eschews semantic alteration entirely. Instead, the new method encodes Trojan payloads within the semantics of the host image by utilizing under-exploited model vulnerabilities. Although initial performance indicates that these hostless Trojans induce superior effectiveness compared to their host-dependent counterparts at equivalent trigger sizes, their ability to evade standard detection systems remains a concern. To address this, the work proposes a more intricate trigger design that balances high stealth with effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both efficacy and stealthiness. Furthermore, the research establishes a new category of "Hostless Trojans" and provides the necessary theoretical framework for understanding and countering them.

The Reconfigurable Optics Spectrograph Integral Field Unit (ROSIE) will be integrated with the Magellan Imaging and Spectrograph to transform it into a full integral field spectrometer capable of delivering high-fidelity data for diverse astronomical investigations. Designed to be flexible and easily reconfigured, the system is being built in phases; this abstract details the current status of the optical pathfinder. This prototype features 120 detectors arranged in a 10x12 grid, covering a field of view of 0.7" x 0.67" with a scale of 0.06" mm/mag. It has undergone extensive laboratory testing and on-sky validation using the 6.5m Magellan telescope.

This study examines recent findings regarding carbon-carbon fusion, emphasizing that while significant advancements have been made in recent decades, numerous critical questions remain unresolved. Emphatically, the paper advocates for utilizing the "promoting Trojan horse" methodology to enhance measurement precision of state-to-state cross sections near the Coulomb barrier. Furthermore, it highlights that refining these cross-section measurements are essential for advancing the understanding of the fusion mechanism and for developing more robust theoretical models. Consequently, these improvements are deemed necessary to facilitate future astrophysical calculations of the $^{12}$C+$^{12}$C reaction rates.

We present high-resolution, high-signal-to-noise ratio spectroscopic data for 102 stars hosting planets with masses between 0.3 and 8.2 $M_{\oplus}$. Our analysis measured elemental abundances for C, N, S, Na, Mg, Si, Fe, and Ni, deriving a precision of 0.05–0.2 dex for most elements (except for C and N, which ranged from 0.15 to 0.35). These results enable a robust comparison of stellar compositions, effectively modeling the internal structures of the corresponding terrestrial exoplanets. We found that while the majority of these stars exhibit standard galactic chemical patterns, 12 stars (accounting for 12%) show significant elemental divergences exceeding 1.5 dex relative to solar ratios, suggesting their planetary cores likely contain unusual elemental ratios. We also examined correlations among elements to test for external pollution or internal sequestration mechanisms. Most stars display no evidence of such processes; however, in the 12 polluted systems, specific signatures point to either pollution or core differentiation as the underlying cause. Finally, we explored connections between stellar chemical anomalies and planetary mass, searching for clues about internal structure. We detected no universal trends across the sample, but identified distinct patterns within the subset of 12 polluted stars, indicating that the relationships between anomalous compositions and planetary mass differ depending on whether pollution is present.

Commercial Wireless Positioning (WP) systems utilize Channel State Information (CSI) from Wi-Fi Li-Local area Networking (LiAN) to determine the locations of handheld devices. These advanced protocols depend on a database mapping received signal characteristics to known reference positions within the environment under study. However, when these LiAN Li-Local area Networks operate in open spaces, the performance of commercial WP systems deteriorates significantly. This study enhances Li-Local area Networking based positioning accuracy in open space scenarios by using the "attention" mechanism. The system first extracts "attention" features from raw Channel State Information using the "attention" mechanism. The extracted "attention" features are then fed into the system to build a database of reference positions. The entire process is supervised by the "attention" mechanism. Experimental results show that the proposed system outperforms existing commercial positioning systems in open space scenarios.

We introduce a novel, purely topological category of structures for modal logic as an alternative to standard Kripke frames. In this framework, every relationally defined concept—such as validity, satisfiability, or satisfiability—maps directly to a corresponding property of topological spaces. The logic's axioms are then interpreted as specific constraints within those spatial interpretations, allowing for the development of both a novel semantic theory for modal logom and an unprecedently simple, fully constructive proof system. The formalization makes use of the principles of constructive mathematics.

The notion of edge-tinting on a graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns each edge an integer value, where the absolute discrepancy between the sums of values for any two adjacent edges must sum to no more than a given parameter $m$. A graph is classified as edge-tintable if there exists a parameter $m$ such that at least one valid tinting configuration exists; the edge-tint index of $G$, denoted $\mu(G)$, represents the smallest such $m$. In 2012, Borodin et al. conjectured that all cubic bipartite graphs possess an index of $\mu(G) = 3$. This study presents the first known example of a cubic bipartite graph requiring an index of $\mu(G) = 4$, thereby providing definitive evidence that the conjecture is incorrect.

This study investigates functions on the hypercube $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ with bounded degree and Fourier concentration. We demonstrate a hypergraph-based approach to constructing specific functions with restricted support and provide an alternative perspective on a known result by Linial and Radoicic ($n$). Furthermore, we derive upper limits for the size of support using concepts from uniform sampling and approximate counting. Finally, the concept of "graph connectivity" is defined and examined, along with its relationship to the Samorini-Sarkar-Sinha-Singh (SSSS) network and Hamming networks with specific parameters, as described.

Although the Comprehensive Object-Oriented Simulation Environment for Biochemical Pathways (COPASI) is a robust, multiplatform scientific suite for mathematical modeling of molecular complexes, it lacks a web-based user interface. Consequently, users cannot access its features directly via a browser. This limitation restricts COPASI's availability for those without the software installed and hampers its utility in interactive classroom settings. To address this, a novel web frontend termed ShinyCOPASI has been developed, leveraging a Shiny application to drive a powerful Web Desktop version of COPASI via remote execution. Accessible via a user-friendly graphical GUI, the platform enables the construction, modification, and execution of modeling networks stored on a centralized server, with all specific configurations tailored to the user. Both standalone and remote server deployments are supported, with the Shiny component freely obtainable as an open-source web source.

In Science machine intelligence (SCI), ensuring explainability and understanding within algorithms is crucial for accurately interpreting data, validating models, and effectively communicating results to a broad audience. While developing ambiguity detection tools is essential to enhance SCI explainability, these tools are not yet universally adopted across the community. This paper examines various available approaches, evaluates them against established metrics, and highlights the need for a unified standard to benchmark and compare the performance of different ambiguity detectors. Additionally, it explores future avenues of research and potential advancements in this field.

For a compact quantum group $\mathcal{G}$, we denote by $vN(\mathcal{G})$ its von Neumann algebra. In this paper, we investigate the algebraic properties of $vN(\mathcal{G})$ through its tensor structure and the injectivity of this algebra. Additionally, we explore a specific von Neumann algebra associated with a subset of functions in $C(\mathcal{G})$ that correspond to certain partitions of the quantum group $\mathcal{G}$; this subalgebra is referred to as the von Neumann algebra generated by category functions.

The iteration implicity associated with traditional Gauss-Seidel, Red-Black, White, Black schemes and other techniques can lead to convergence failure in massive-scale problems stemming from Markov chains and discrete Markov decision processes (MDP). To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Imprecise GMRES (IGMRES) that generalizes the standard K-residual minimization method (K-RMM). By integrating the Imprecise Point Evaluation (IPE) concept with K-RMM, IGMRES estimates the convergence behavior prior to full algorithm execution. This predictive capability allows for the adjustment of iteration counts to prevent premature divergence. Additionally, we present an extension capable of handling problems with multiple states. Comprehensive experiments on extensive-state-space problems demonstrate that IGMRES delivers superior solutions compared to the fixed-iteration version of K-RMM.

This paper symbolically decomposes the ideals associated with the common edge complements of weighted directed graphs. A central component of our decomposition is the ideal $J(G)$, which represents the set of all edges that share a vertex with at least one other edge in a given directed loop (this set is not necessarily transitive). We demonstrate a duality where the algebraic multiplicity of $J(G)$ depends exclusively on the number of vertices with an in-degree of zero and an out-degree of zero. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial definition for the ideal generated by $J(G)$ based on the structural properties of the underlying graph. Finally, we define a class of ideals with these properties that are perfect for commutative algebraic analysis, specifically in terms of their projective dimensions and Cohen-Macaulay status.

Computer simulations frequently serve as a primary avenue for investigating complex phenomena across the physical and life sciences. However, the intricate mechanisms underlying these models often introduce complexities that traditional statistical methods struggle to manage. This study introduces novel techniques designed to identify and characterize the drivers within time series data generated by simulations. Our approach integrates multiple contour mapping methods with a specific analysis of covariance aimed at multivariate time series. These simulations were executed in both univariate and multivariate forms to validate the proposed methods, demonstrating their efficacy in identifying simulated drivers across diverse time series configurations.

The core challenge in distributed machine learning is data poisoning, which compromises the integrity of distributed systems. While geographic region queries are commonly used to scale these networks, they can also be exploited by attackers to amplify the impact of poison attacks. This paper investigates the conditions under which region queries either help or hinder resistance against such attacks. Our findings indicate that, contrary to earlier assumptions about automatic security benefits, region queries are only more favorable for resilience when the number of poisoned data samples in each area is kept small. Additionally, we derive a new Poisson-based approach to attack detection and query management, demonstrating through experiments that this method offers robust protection with minimal false positives.

This study examines jet fragmentation within central Pb-Pb interactions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV utilizing jets tagged by isolated photons. By analyzing the hadronic substructure relative to the photon, we effectively disentangle the medium's influence from initial-state effects. The observed shift in the median of the photon-jet $\zeta$ distribution toward lower values as system centrality increases confirms that the heavy medium significantly modifies hadron fragmentation.

In 2019, the M8.5 dwarf WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 (hereafter W1534-1043) was identified as a T/Y transition object exhibiting a pronounced, anomalous absorption feature in the 3.3-$\mu$m band, which has proven difficult to account for using standard molecular bands. This study presents comprehensive $u$-band data from the MMT Observatory, alongside $J$, $H$, and $K$-band spectra from the VLT, which were fitted using the M8.5 dwarf WD1452+53 as a reference. Our analysis indicates that the anomalous feature arises from a combination of the M8.5 species, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, and $\mathrm{NH_3}$. Furthermore, we utilized the M8.5 object WD1452+53 for spectral fitting and identified the 3.3-$\mu$m feature as resulting from a combination of the M8.5 species, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, and $\mathrm{NH_3}$. Our analysis indicates that the anomalous feature arises from a combination of the M8.5 species, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, and $\mathrm{NH_3}$. This study reports the production yields of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons utilizing central collisions data from xenon atoms, recorded by the Topological Tracking Xenon (ATLAS) experiment at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of 1.46 $\mathrm{mb}^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. Meson species were identified through decays into pairs of charged particles, while proton and anti-proton species were distinguished using specific momentum-dependent identification techniques.

Parton distribution functions (PDFs) are essential tools in hadron collider physics, utilized for predicting collision event rates in both proton-proton and lepton-proton collisions. These functions are conventionally fitted to experimental datasets using a specific parametric framework, with parameters refined through a global analysis. However, as collider luminosity rises and dataset sizes expand, the traditional, periodic refitting process becomes increasingly costly and inefficient. Consequently, there is a growing need for more agile alternatives that can efficiently leverage new data as it accumulates. This paper introduces a methodology for progressively and N-exactly parton distribution functions using novel "base" functions. These fitted functions are optimized against historical datasets and are subsequently updated with new data in real time. The approach is validated through numerical simulations applied to both hypothetical PDFs and the MST2018 model using N-exponential and N-Gauss approximations, as well as N-exponential and N-Gauss representations of the MST2018 model. Numerical simulations applied to both hypothetical PDFs and the MST2018 model using N-exponential and N-Gauss representations of the MST2018 model.

Sintering stands as a primary mechanism for the development of macropores and cemented structures within regolith on the Moon and Mars. As an extensive, continuous, and heat-conducting layer, this rocky debris facilitates the transmission of thermal energy from the surface, particularly during the heating cycles of the solar day. While the extent to which solar heating impacts sintering remains uncertain, it is a critical variable. This study examines how such heating influences regolith properties by conducting experiments that compacted simulated lunar and Martian soils, subsequently subjecting them to cycling temperatures representing the Martian solar day and subsequent analysis of their microstructural and mechanical characteristics. The research evaluates the effects of initial compaction pressure and thermal processing, as well as the inherent differences between simulated materials, by analyzing porosity, mean particle diameter, density, compressive strength, and elastic modulus. Results indicate that solar-scale temperature fluctuations significantly alter these attributes, demonstrating that while the final microstructure and mechanical behavior of the two simulated regoliths diverge, both are substantially influenced by the thermal cycle.

The surface of the Earth is predominantly covered by water, and the dynamics of liquid surfaces have been the subject of extensive study. A classic example in this field is the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, which causes a free-standing liquid cylinder to break up into droplets. In contrast, when this instability affects liquid layers confined between two parallel plates, it leads to the formation of liquid droplets or a banded pattern, a phenomenon that has been thoroughly analyzed. This study introduces a novel intermediate system: a liquid layer situated on a solid fiber. This setup represents a previously unexamined domain, bridging the gap between Rayleigh-Plateau instability on open surfaces and that on cylindrical ones. We provide analytical predictions for the most probable breakup mode of this liquid layer, an outcome derived from minimizing surface energy. Energy minimization indicates that a bare fiber supports only a single mode, whereas a coated fiber permits multiple modes, with the available options increasing as slip at the liquid-solid interface intensifies. Our findings are validated through direct numerical simulations performed on the governing Navier-Stokes equations. These simulations corroborate the analytical findings and further reveal an additional secondary instability occurring within the primary breakup droplets.

The $\lambda$-test utilizes the ratio of the rest-frame 4.05 $\mu$m ($\lambda$-em) luminosity to the Stefan-Boltzmann radius ($R_{\rm bol}$) as a proxy for the star formation rate (SFR). This test is considered most effective for young galaxies where dust-reprocessed emission is negligible. This study introduces an alternative $\lambda$-test based on the ratio of $L_{3.73}/L_{\rm bol}$ (where 3.73 refers to the 3.73 $\mu$m band), which offers a benchmark for testing the SFR estimates derived from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. This approach involves comparing the results of this new $\lambda$-test with those of the original to evaluate the accuracy of the SED-derived SFRs.

Diffusion models have recently emerged as a significant advancement in generative deep learning, achieving state-of-the-art results in high-resolution image synthesis across various domains. This paper introduces a distinct, theoretically grounded methodology for universal diffusion applicable to both forward and reverse processes. The framework addresses universal diffusion by formulating these processes through input-output pairs, existence and uniqueness theorems, and a dynamic model grounded in stochastic analysis. For the forward dynamic, we demonstrate that a uniquely determined continuous path exists, defined by an auxiliary time-inhomogeneous potential; this potential simultaneously drives the process and the reverse dynamic. In the auxiliary potential, we propose a novel data-driven estimation technique. Experimental results confirm that the framework effectively synthesizes images at 512×512 resolution on the Gen-3X dataset, with the universal diffusion achieving state-of-the-art quality comparable to other leading models.

Recognizing handwritten mathematical formulas is vital for preserving historical scientific literature and accelerating knowledge discovery. Although current optical character recognition tools struggle with the unique complexities of mathematical symbols, this study introduces a novel system for accurately transcribing handwritten formulas on paper. By leveraging 15 pen-mounted sensors that capture stroke dynamics—including pressure, speed, and movement trajectories—the research utilizes sensor-derived data to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). This approach achieved an accuracy of 96.6% in a blind test against human performance levels of 98.6%, effectively demonstrating the efficacy of analyzing stroke features for mathematical expression identification.

This paper introduces a novel technique for generating synthetic speech durations in mid-fundamental frequency (MDF) levels, designed to replace traditional co-ordinate or parametric synthesis methods like statistical parametric audio (SPS). Unlike these co-ordinate systems, which rely on extensive datasets for training, our non-empirical approach offers a significant advantage by eliminating the need for pre-training. For the proposed framework, we first establish a table of average speech lengths across distinct phonemes and acoustic characteristics. Subsequently, we utilize this static audio to model duration variations in synthetic speech. Our statistical analysis demonstrates performance on par with, and in some cases superior to, existing statistical methods. Furthermore, we provide a web-based demonstration available at https://www.cstr.ed.ac.uk/projects/mdf/speech_duration/.

Spatially explicit models are increasingly utilized in ecology to analyze how presence-absence or abundance data vary across a continuum of locations. While this approach offers several advantages over traditional non-spatial methods, it demands careful consideration of spatial autocorrelation to avoid issues such as inflated Type I error rates, overdispersion, and overlooked spatial heterogeneity. The **spHabitat** R package is designed to analyze single-species, multi-species, and integrated datasets using Presence models. These models incorporate spatial components into the traditional habitat relationship framework to account for autocorrelation and spatial variability. The package provides maximum likelihood estimation for these scenarios, including the capability to integrate data sources. For model selection, spHabitat utilizes an information-theoretic approach that offers alternative theoretical frameworks and spatial kernels, including the option of comparing these models to null (non-spatial) alternatives. Furthermore, it includes functions for assessing model performance and validating results through cross-validation.

Skin lesions are a primary source of dermatologist visits, and the DermoLearn initiative aims to support this field by offering a vast repository of high-quality, diverse clinical images alongside advanced segmentation and classification pre-trained models. DermoLearn functions as a versatile platform that caters to multiple user needs: it provides clinicians with access to extensive pathology visuals for education, enables researchers to utilize these datasets for custom studies, and offers machine learning experts pre-trained algorithms to streamline their work.

We introduce a stochastic autoencoder designed to analyze multi-band optical and near-infrared data from Type Ia supernovae, offering a unified framework for addressing both classification and regression challenges. By integrating probabilistic elements, the approach effectively captures inherent uncertainties in the data, offering significant potential for advancements in analyzing incomplete spectra and developing improved incomplete data imputation techniques. Furthermore, the derived latent representations facilitate the construction of an efficient supernova spectrum interpolator. When assessed on publicly available datasets, these generated latent variables deliver superior performance for estimating the supernova absolute magnitude compared to utilizing raw spectra directly.

We present high-resolution spectroscopic observations of the $[NII]\lambda\lambda$ 6548, 6553, 6570, 6580 Å emission lines for a gravitationally lensed, star-forming galaxy at a redshift of $z=2.09$. Our kinematic analysis reveals that this system exhibits a rotating disk with an inclination of $i=63^\circ$ and a major-axis rotation velocity of $v_{rot}=220\pm 10$ km s$^{-1}$. The observed rotation curve displays a double-peaked structure, attributed to a combination of non-Keplerian behavior and the intrinsic line profile shape, with a de-projected major-axis velocity of $v_{rot}=220\pm 10$ km s$^{-1}$ and a slight outflow component of $v_{out}=100$ km s$^{-1}$. The kinematic axis ratio is measured as $q=0.55$, though the observed line profile width ratio of $q=0.4$ reflects the influence of a point-mass lens. This study examines the dynamics of turbulent, neutral plumes using both direct numerical simulations and large-eddy simulations, with a specific focus on how particles with finite but negligible inertia behave. The results indicate that such particles are incorporated into the plumes at an elevated rate compared to the fluid alone, a phenomenon driven by the interaction between particle-laden plumes and ambient air. This interaction generates vorticity and distortion at the interface, which enhances the entrainment process. The study quantifies the additional entrainment by analyzing the relationship between the enhanced mass flux and the virtual density deficit. Furthermore, the excess mass flux is linked to the variance of virtual buoyancy, which is determined by the particle Stokes number and the density ratio, representing the ambient-to-buoyant density.

The propagation of infectious diseases within a population is frequently modeled as a stochastic process influenced by a contact network, where each node signifies an individual and each edge denotes an interaction. In this work, we examine such processes on hypergraphs—structures comprising multi-ended edges representing intricate, high-order interactions among groups of people. Our primary aim is to establish spectral bounds that dictate the extinction probability of infected states. Specifically, we identify spectral characteristics of hypergraphs that constrain the lowest eigenvalue of transition matrices for infectious states, thereby determining the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) for the system. When $R_0$ falls below unity, the infection state becomes ergodic, guaranteeing disease extinction; conversely, if $R_0$ exceeds this threshold, persistent infections may spread. By situating our methodology within the framework of stochastic linear programming, we derive a novel set of spectral constraints applicable to any hypergraph. These findings are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs and demonstrated through both analytical reasoning and numerical simulations.

The magnetic properties of the 2D ferromagnetic insulator CrI$_3$ are significantly influenced by the magnetic field's orientation in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling. This study employs density functional theory to analyze the magnetic behavior of a bilayer CrI$_3$ subjected to out-of-plane fields, revealing that while temperature is negligible, in-plane fields can disrupt long-range magnetic order, with effects intensifying as the Rashba parameter rises. Specifically, we observe that an upward-pointing in-plane field strengthens interactions to produce a parallel antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state, whereas a downward-pointing one enhances them to favor an antidirectional AFM arrangement. Furthermore, our spin-Schmidt analysis indicates that the magnetic moment's $z$-component dominates, while the $\delta$-component of the spin magnetization drives the distinct switching between parallel and antiparallel AFM states caused by the direction of the applied field.

The study explores the characteristics of magnetic activity cycles in systems featuring differential, anti-solar trends, a topic of particular relevance for active Kepler stars, including the well-monitored K2-3 system. Simulated-to-Real (Sim2Real) translation represents a critical yet difficult challenge for deep learning-based navigation systems. This challenge evaluates methods designed to handle difficult cases in Natural Language Understanding, specifically targeting items not found in the lexicon, such as rare words, unfamiliar jargon, or content outside a system's current knowledge base. The focus is assessing how these rare or out-of-vocabulary items impact performance. The Synonym task targets in-vocab items, while the Numerical Extraction task targets out-of-vocab items. The final selection is determined by the best performing model from this initial phase, which then executes both tasks on both in-vocab and out-vocab test sets. This study presents an efficient, easy-to-implement, and robust methodology for verifying stochastic finite element models that rely on generalized polynomial chaos expansions, targeting a specified level of confidence. The approach addresses the risk of model failures stemming from undisclosed stochastic dependencies, particularly those caused by uncontrolled small stochastic integration step sizes, which can cause spectral expansions to converge to incorrect limits rather than true probability density functions. By adapting techniques from deterministic non-conforming finite element analysis, our method post-processes standard stochastic simulations by introducing projection into a higher-order polynomial space. Through comparison of spectral coefficients at coarsely spaced random variable evaluation points, discrepancies are detected and quantified. The authors demonstrate the utility of this framework across three representative cases: a stochastic heat conduction problem, non-conforming deterministic models, and analyses involving random fields.

The sequential alteration identification and isolation (SAII) framework enables online detection of significant distribution shifts within data streams, a critical capability for applications such as intrusion detection and medical monitoring. In many practical scenarios, however, access to streams is constrained by costs or technical limitations, necessitating research into partially-observed data streams where only a subset is available. This paper introduces a novel approach for these partially observed settings that permits decision-making based on adaptive sampling strategies. Determining when to modify a model at minimal sampling intervals is a complex challenge. To address this, the proposed algorithm employs a D-optimization criterion that estimates the information gain regarding alteration parameters achieved through sampling. Further, an enhanced algorithm utilizing an augmented dataset constructed via imputation is developed. Empirical evaluations confirm that this method outperforms existing techniques across both fully and partially observed data stream environments.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on the chemical abundances of 1,000 metal-poor dwarf galaxies, utilizing the R2K2 project's data from the LAMOST survey. Our analysis focused on mean chemical abundances, dispersion values, and abundance ratios, particularly [Fe/H], [α/Fe], and [Fe/ Mg]. The resulting distributions for both the mean trends and dispersion in [Fe/H] and [α/Fe] across these galaxies are nearly Gaussian, with a very slight skew toward lower metallicities. We identified three distinct evolutionary patterns for [α/Fe] relative to [Fe/H]: the majority of galaxies (80%) show a rapid initial rise in [α/Fe] that peaks at [Fe/H] ≈ -1.0 before declining; a smaller subset (15%) exhibits a more gradual, continuous increase; and a minority (5%) display flat or irregular variations. The observed mean trends and dispersion profiles, whether Gaussian or defined by these evolutionary types, are primarily governed by the number of stellar generations and the timing of chemical enrichment, respectively. The evolution of [Fe/ Mg] specifically reflects the yields from core-collapse supernovae versus the delay in releasing elemental iron, with the latter determined by the merger of white dwarf binaries in galactic central regions. Building accurate models for visual documents, which include images, tables, and text, demands complex multi-modal architectures. Developing such systems typically requires extensive, costly labeling efforts for both layouts and content. To address this, we present an approach that merges automatic and efficient annotation tools with transfer learning, enabling the creation of high-performance multi-modal extraction systems while drastically cutting down annotation expenses. We validated this strategy using real-world scenarios to extract data from licenses and invoices, demonstrating that our method produces superior models compared to pure end-to-end alternatives and significantly outperforms manual labeling in cost-efficiency.

Training deep neural networks (DNNs) using deep learning frameworks is resource-intensive, particularly when employing memory-hungry and computally demanding operations like convolutions. Although network pruning can enhance both memory usage and computational efficiency, traditional methods often fail to retain the original architecture, leading to significant semantic gaps between the pruned model and its full-precision counterpart. This discrepancy necessitates extensive retraining and fine-tuning to achieve satisfactory accuracy. We introduce a new, precise end-to-end pruning technique called **ClickTrain**, designed specifically to generate highly DNN-architecturally similar pruned models. This approach eliminates the need for retraining or fine-tuning while accelerating DNN training substantially. ClickTrain operates by applying targeted, fine-grained pruning to individual operator sub-components—such as reducing channel counts in specific layers of a convolutional matrix or decreasing feature map dimensions in pooling layers—preserving the overall structural integrity of the network. Furthermore, an integrated co-design methodology allows ClickTrain to optimize pruning strategies according to specific hardware constraints. Experimental results on standard ImageNet DNN benchmarks demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves performance improvements of up to **2.3× in memory** and **10.8× in computation** compared to competing methods, all without compromising accuracy or requiring additional retraining efforts.

The merger of neutron stars and black holes represents the most prevalent channel for generating gravitational waves, yet current detection methods rely heavily on template-based matched filtering, which is constrained by uncertainties regarding the neutron star equation of state and the inability to cover the entire parameter space efficiently. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify and classify these events, aiming to surpass the limitations inherent in traditional matched filtering. The proposed model, DN-SNAP, integrates two core components: a classification module that distinguishes between binary neutron star, binary black hole, and single-object signals, and a secondary module that extracts physical properties such as component masses, spins, and redshifts. DN-SNAP processes time and frequency domain waveform data as input, achieving classification accuracy of 99.99% and mean absolute error below 0.15 for the estimated parameters. Additionally, we present an automated system for identifying potential mismodeling issues caused by numerical artifacts or unanticipated physical effects.

The planet exhibits an inclination of 87.2° and completes an orbit at an average semi-major axis of 0.047 AU, reaching periastron distances of roughly 0.023 AU. This discovery represents the first confirmed exoplanet with such significant eccentricity to be identified by TESS. Additionally, the system's age is estimated between 8.2 and 8.9 billion years, placing it in the oldest category of known host stars for gas giants.

Assuming a constant dissipation rate, our analysis reveals a novel asymptotic fixed point representing a dissipative de Sitter universe. We further demonstrate that this de Sitter state can coexist with the matter-dominated era, thereby bridging the typically abrupt transition between matter domination and de Sitter expansion. Additionally, this proposed model addresses the theoretical challenges of the cosmological constant's magnitude and sign issues.

We provide a direct demonstration of the ill-posedness of the incompressible Euler equations (both with zero vorticity and otherwise) within critical Sobolev spaces $H^{1}$ (and more generally $H^{s}$ for $s \geq 1$) by leveraging existing null controllability results. Specifically, we exploit the capability to steer certain energetically constrained initial states to rest in finite time to establish that final states lacking uniqueness cannot be zero.

Grasshopper is a universal neural network framework designed for reversible image steganography, offering graph-based uncertainty to guide training. By employing the KL-Bayesian neural network as a modifier, Grasshopper enhances the reliability of the output. Additionally, it optimizes the hybrid loss function to enhance prediction accuracy and accelerates the training process through the Adam optimizer. Testing on the COCO dataset using 512 × 512 images with an embedding capacity of 0.2 bits per pixel demonstrated that this approach surpasses current methods. Specifically, it achieves superior accuracy and a PSNR of 48.58 dB.

Magnetic luminous spots are a form of solar activity that can be modeled as distributions of magnetic flux. This paper provides observational evidence supporting a two-part distribution model for these regions, characterized by fields of approximately 1,500 Gauss and roughly 3,000 Gauss. The study utilizes observational data from the Solar Optical Telescope on board the JAXA/Japan's Heliophysics Satellite, SuMI, which captured the sun's visible light. This allows for the precise counting of flux points at a spatial resolution of roughly 18 kilometers. Observational data from the Solar Optical Telescope on board the JAXA's Heliophysics Satellite, which has a spatial resolution of approximately 18 kilometers, allows for the precise determination of flux point distributions. This high spatial precision enables the observation that the distribution of flux points is not random but follows a specific pattern. This pattern is well-explained by assuming the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic regions with field strengths of roughly 1,500 Gauss and 3,000 Gauss.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest within artificial intelligence regarding the visual identification of humans, driven by applications spanning security and surveillance to social networking and content moderation. While neural networks have proven highly successful in this area, they often fail in specific contexts, prompting a closer examination by artists and designers who explore how objects, scenes, and lighting can alter a person's appearance. Human expertise in visual ID is also vulnerable to similar limitations; individual perceptual strategies vary greatly, and cognitive biases can lead experts to base judgments on incidental film features—such as background scenery or attire—rather than facial characteristics. This study explores the capabilities and limitations of visual ID systems through the lens of human capabilities, specifically analyzing how minimalist visual elements either support or hinder ID tasks by comparing the focus of experts with that of non-experts in both practice and theory.

We conclude that a MSO composed of neutral milli-magnetic monopoles dark matter (mMM) can effectively explain the observed dynamics of both the Earth and the Milky Way Galaxy. In the case of the Earth, we show that the end force of mMM on a singly charged electron is roughly 10 Newtons (N), a magnitude sufficient to counteract gravitational pull. For the Milky Way, the end force of mMM on an proton is approximately $10^{-3}$ dynes, which is large enough to sustain the observed kinetic energies of galactic gas and stars within the galaxy.

Accurately forecasting spatio-temporal climate patterns is vital for addressing global environmental concerns, yet existing methods often fail to effectively capture complex local structures or intricate dependencies. To address this gap, we introduce T-XInet, a novel network designed for superior spatial-temporal modeling. First, T-XInet employs a local 2-D shift-window mechanism that divides input data into non-overlapping blocks, allowing the cross-focus layer to capture interactions across window boundaries while maintaining computational efficiency. Second, it utilizes a window-wise self-attention mechanism to feature extraction within each block, facilitating the capture of deep spatial and temporal rules without incurring spatial displacement. Third, a new window-reconstruction module is incorporated to further enhance the representation of local features. Evaluations across two extensive real-world datasets confirm the model's effectiveness, demonstrating that T-XInet surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in forecasting real-spatio-temporal signals.

We introduce two shadow matter scenarios within a three-Higgs-doublet framework characterized by $S_3$ symmetry, where the first model extends the scalar sector of Type-II two-Higgs-doublet models (Type-II 2HDM) and the second offers greater complexity as a variant of Type-IIl 2HDM. In both cases, the added scalar doublets serve specifically to satisfy the muon $g-2$ anomaly. We thoroughly examine the mass spectra and couplings specific to the scalar sectors. Furthermore, we assess experimental viability against current constraints on scalars and the muon $g-2$ anomaly utilizing the software tool HiggsNext. Our analysis indicates that while both models remain viable under existing bounds, predicting a single heavy scalar mass spectrum is common across both. Specifically, we find that a $Z\to \tau \bar{\tau}$ decay channel could enable detection of one or two of these scalars at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) with an integrated luminosity of $300 \, fb^{-1}$.

In this study, a PDE-constrained optimization framework is employed to simulate ion transport regulation within a neuronal cell, accounting for congestion effects. The model is built upon a pore solution framework featuring mobile ions and macromolecules confined to the membrane interface, where each component is assigned a congestion coefficient influencing the osmotic activity of mixtures. Through the derivation of the adjoint equations, a sensitivity analysis of the congestion coefficient's impact on ion distribution is conducted. The analysis reveals that increasing the congestion coefficient drives ions toward the membrane membrane, thereby reducing their volume average concentration, while simultaneously causing macro-olecular accumulation in the bulk to increase. An L2-norm objective function is defined to represent an ideal equilibrium state of ion homeostasis in the cytosol, leading to an augmented Lagrangian function for which a finite difference scheme yields solutions. The computational algorithm is implemented in the open-source software package CHOCOLATE4, where simulations demonstrate that achieving the desired homeostatic conditions necessitates a shift away from congestion toward higher membrane localization of macromolecules.

The paper introduces "NeMo," a new approach for identifying influential nodes within social networks. NeMo stands out by leveraging the network's structural motifs—specifically tripartite and quadrilateral motifs—to rank node importance. We found that these motifs provide deeper insights into the network's topology than traditional methods like degree centrality or betweenness. Experiments on real datasets confirm NeMo's effectiveness in locating key nodes across various scenarios, including detecting new members, identifying fraudsters, and pinpointing individuals who recruit others into criminal activities.

We have conducted the first comprehensive analysis of a white dwarf spiraling into a black hole, utilizing the white dwarf's final explosion as a novel, model-driven method to determine the system's orbital separation. This approach capitalizes on detectable deviations in the radio emission generated by ionized material stripped from the white dwarf during the final descent. The study reveals that the optimal distance for isolating the orbital signature lies within approximately 10% of the black hole's event horizon. At these extreme separations, the orbital signal manifests as rapid, periodic fluctuations with amplitudes reaching up to 100% in the observed flux.

Deblurring deformed images, a widespread issue in both indoor and outdoor settings, has been the focus of this study. While traditional methods often fail to deliver satisfactory results on real-world data due to challenges with occlusion dynamics and scene motion, this paper introduces a new deep learning approach. We introduced a pseudo-blur conditional generator designed to create synthetic blurry images that match the specific motion patterns found within actual de degraded inputs. This blurry template is then utilized as a guide for a translation network responsible for recovering the sharp corresponding region. By generating dynamic and realistic-looking blur templates, the method can effectively decompose movements and accurately restore these areas without being constrained by fixed blurred backgrounds found in prior techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed approach achieves superior performance over existing state-of-the-art methods when restoring images from genuine real-world data.

This study introduces a new model of spiking neurons based on molecular mechanisms that incorporate both ion channel dynamics and the physical movement of ions. The model employs two types of ions and three distinct channels: a voltage-gated channel governed by the activation equilibrium with its corresponding inverse, an inverse representing passive diffusion, and an additional gated channel utilizing similar on/off equilibrium dynamics. By formulating the system with these components, the researchers demonstrated that the core principles of the "conductance-based" Hodgkin-Huxley neuron can be effectively replicated at the molecular scale. Furthermore, the model exhibits intrinsic conductance-type adaptivity conductance, enabling the deployment of adaptive exponential spiking neurons. The proposed structure is exceptionally simple in terms of both ions and channels while ensuring that the mathematical framework for time-evolving variables remains first-order. Due to this low molecular complexity and the suitability of the variable orders for biochemical simulation techniques, the model can be translated into system of ordinary differential equations suitable for agent programming. Consequently, these constructed spiking neurons are capable of emulating more complex Hodgkin-Huxley neurons through the methodology of direct simulation programming.

The paper provides a characterization of thoroughness in ordered sets via interval sequences. Additionally, it examines sequences of real numbers using ordered tuple structures to develop specific criteria determining the property of the resulting ultrapower.

The rise of machine learning has generated an explosion in data, resulting in numerous datasets that are increasingly incompatible with one another. This incompatibility stems from differences in data types, missing links between domains, varying schemas, and distinct data collection processes, all of which hinder effective data fusion and knowledge transfer. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of "dataset uniqueness," defined as the distinct, non-overlapping information contained within a dataset that cannot currently be accessed through other sources. We also propose the methodology of dataset unique profiling, which involves calculating this unique contribution for every attribute relative to a set of comparable datasets. Our findings, which apply to a collection of 1,153 datasets across 10 domains, indicate that domain-unique information is substantially more prevalent than dataset-wide unique data. However, when examining specific attributes, the dataset-level unique data dominates. These insights have significant implications for data integration, enabling more strategic approaches to merging data and reducing redundancy, as well as enhancing semantic web technologies by facilitating better inference and the closure of knowledge graphs.

In 1965, Gales conjectured that any $n$-chromatic graph on at least $\binom{2n - \text{chrom}}{2}$ vertices must contain a complete subgraph of size $n - \text{chrom} + 1$. This paper improves this hypothesis specifically for graphs with $4$ and $5$ colors. Additionally, a full characterization is provided of all $2$-sparse graphs with $n$ colors that do not contain a clique of size $n - \text{chrom} + 1$.

This paper proposes a generalized correntropy-based sturdy smooth graph signal recovery (AGCR) technique that utilizes robust kernel functions and simultaneously optimally adjusts the correntropy kernel width through an online data-driven approach. Initially, the proposed method ensures reliable recovery by integrating the $l_{2}$-norm into the cost function to diminish the impact of outliers on graph nodes and their connections. Subsequently, a fast kernel adaptation method (KACLA) is employed to automatically determine the optimal correntropy kernel $w^*$, thereby enhancing the AGCR algorithm's nonparametric robustness. Furthermore, by leveraging the specific properties of the AGCR and KACLA structures, we establish the convergence characteristics of both the $l_{2}$-norm and generalized correntropy-based schemes within the domain of graph signal processing. Finally, the efficacy of the new approach is validated through simulations and actual real-world experiments, demonstrating superior performance in noisy environments with impulsive interference.

We introduce a method for generating custom-designed quantum states within an entangled spinor interferometer, utilizing two key variables: the total number of particles involved and their entanglement degree. These parameters are manipulated to optimize a specific quantity, defined as the ratio of a signal's contrast to the noise level from the detector. This ratio is calculated using an efficient, numerically stable algorithm. Our method allows for the simulation of advanced techniques, such as those employed in large-scale atom interferometers, by entangling more particles and producing tailored states. The results demonstrate that using custom-constructed, rather than simply maximally entangled, states consistently yields a higher signal-to-noise ratio. These approaches are implemented in actual experiments and have been used to measure optimal outcomes.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have proven highly effective across diverse applications, yet the specifics of their convolutional operations and their innate suitability for graph-structured data remain unclear. This study addresses that gap by introducing Fractional Diffusion (FD), a technique that formulates graph convolution as a strategic enhancement of spectral filters to replicate graph convolutions of any order. Notably, the output coefficients of GCNNs of a specific convolution order $k$ align precisely with the $k$-th derivative of the FD output. Additionally, we developed an algorithm to determine GCNN filter coefficients by analytically linking them to the intrinsic attributes of graphs and their attributes. Finally, our empirical results demonstrate a strong correlation between GCNN convolution orders and fractional derivatives, verifying that increasing convolution order amplifies spatial sensitivity in feature extraction while simultaneously reducing frequency components.

Context plays a pivotal role in understanding language, yet real-world applications often face challenges where relevant background context is unavailable. While transfer learning has been employed to acquire context from external sources, these methods typically demand substantial amounts of labeled data. To address this, we introduce the Profound Contextualized Self-learning (PCSL) pipeline, designed to function effectively with minimal external dependencies. PCSL integrates self-training with specialized pre-training strategies to harness unlabelled resources. Our system was trained and validated using the ProPublica Comorbidities dataset, achieving a 40.5% accuracy rate with only 10,000 labeled samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate the specific contributions of each proposed component through a series of ablation studies.

This approach utilizes a single input parameter, the quark mass, which is determined by matching the model's prediction for the pseudoscalar meson mass against experimental values. The theoretical framework derives meson wave functions from the eigenstates of the light-front quark model's light-cone Hamiltonian. Notably, these wave functions exhibit a logarithmic singularity at the boundary, which is a direct outcome of enforcing meson mass constraints. The model's validity is confirmed by its ability to predict the $B	o D\ell^+\ell^-
u_\ell$ decay rate in agreement with experimental observations. Furthermore, the study provides implications for the extraction of the CKM matrix element $|V_{cb}|$ from semileptonic $B	o D\ell^+\ell^-
u_\ell$ decay data.

In the context of Type I string theory, we demonstrate that D-branes possessing $\frac{1}{2}$-fractional half-twisted supersymmetry can be paired to form a single physical brane exhibiting no supersymmetry fractionation. Furthermore, we show that this composite brane manifests $\frac{1}{2}$-fractional supersymmetry itself, with the capacity to be isolated into two distinct components through a non-reversible symmetry transformation. While the brane's components cannot be individually supersymmetric, their collective system preserves supersymmetry. We present a thorough analysis of half-twisted supersymmetry and its role in constructing these D-branes, with particular emphasis on the $\Omega^-$-orientifold projection. As a specific application, our framework provides a novel theoretical basis for the Witten boundary condition.

In 2016, the papers by Cai, Fürer, and Immerman introduced a fundamental result in the field of polynomial time computation. They demonstrated the non-algorithmic separation between the configuration counts of two distinct graphs, even in a scenario where a polynomial relationship between them theoretically exists. In our research, we introduce a different pair of graphs that replicate the original Cai, Fürer, and Immerman properties but possess specific structural attributes. Our graphs are not only disjoint and evidence the same computational separation as the earlier pair, but they also admit efficient algorithms to produce a polynomial relationship between their total counts. Additionally, our separation relies on a separation between the groups defined by these graphs' automorphisms. Finally, we provide a detailed description of the general framework used to construct such pairs of graphs.

The pyrochlore iridates Eu$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and (Eu$_{0.5}$Bi$_{0.5}$)$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ serve as prototypical Mott insulators characterized by strong electron-electron repulsion, magnetic frustration, and the absence of long-range magnetic ordering. In this study, we utilized hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to analyze the electronic states of (Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_{x}$)$_{2}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$ with x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8. Our findings reveal that increasing bismuth doping systematically reduces the degree of Mott insulation. This trend correlates with the enhanced hybridization between Eu and Ir 5d orbitals driven by Bi substitution, which facilitates a transition from an insulating to a metallic state.

This work introduces the "center" and the "boundary" of a two-dimensional data structure, defining them as the respective interior and exterior of its complement within the plane. We investigate their topological properties, dimensions, and whether they remain unchanged under homeomorphism. Additionally, we address two primary research questions: (1) under what conditions do set-valued functions exhibit Lipschitz continuity in their selections? (2) When those conditions are satisfied, how can one explicitly generate a Lipschitz continuous chosen outcome? We answer these by establishing new existence theorems regarding Lipschitz continuity for sets located in two-dimensional spaces and by outlining practical algorithms for doing so. These methods apply broadly, covering scenarios ranging from simple convex forms to intricate image-based functions.

This study investigates the possibility of nontransitivity within circular configurations, specifically examining circular prospects under likelihood ordering. The authors define circular prospects and provide two distinct criteria for likelihood ordering: one based on second-order stochastic dominance and the other on mean-variance. Using these frameworks, the paper presents nontransitive arrangements of circular prospects, with the findings illustrated empirically through simulations. Furthermore, the manuscript explores the implications of these discoveries for the circulation of bets and the formation of markets involving these prospects.

Although modern CPU caches are generally considered sufficient, research indicates that pre-caching data prior to its arrival can yield further performance gains. One approach involves adding extra on-chip memory, yet this merely shifts the bottleneck from L3 to L2/L1 caches and incurs higher costs. Alternatively, reducing the frequency of cache misses by moving setup data onto the processor yields benefits. This paper investigates the potential of relocating run-time established data, which is currently in the global (L3) cache, to smaller, faster on-chip storage. While the runtime nature of this data typically makes such an idea problematic, the paper demonstrates that the data originates from a limited pool of candidates. Consequently, the problem of determining the optimal cache entry for the run-time variable is transformed into a selective fetch of the correct candidate during compile-time. Since the variables are determined dynamically, the specific candidate to pre-cache is a function of the decision logic used at runtime. Consequently, pre-caching these variables alongside the decision logic is necessary. The study concludes that the problem of pre-caching these variables is best addressed by utilizing the existing decision tree structure, specifically by annotating each candidate with the corresponding decision path. The paper presents a methodology for performing this specialisation process, which includes identifying all runtime variables, determining their candidate ranges, gathering execution profiles to identify the most frequent candidates, and implementing candidate range lookup. Direct detection experiments are currently investigating the possibility of low-mass sub-GeV dark matter interacting with nuclear targets. Because such lightweight particles transfer insufficient recoil energy to generate standard nuclear recoil signals, researchers are turning to novel mechanisms like dark matter scattering off nucleons followed by excitation of nuclear de-exciting via electron emission or similar processes. In this study, we examine how accurately one can reconstruct the original dark matter's mass and velocity from the emitted electron's energy and angular distribution. Our findings reveal that even accounting for significant final state uncertainties, the reconstruction of both mass and velocity is highly precise. Consequently, this allows a standard direct detection framework to be applied effectively to infer these original properties from electron spectra. We examine energy entanglement and state transitions within the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, utilizing a photon counter that exhibits sub-Poissonian statistics. Our numerical investigations explore Rabi oscillations, entanglement dynamics, and the probability of photon transmission. These results are compared against those from the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model.

This study presents a new approach for Inter-Beat Interval (IBI) estimation using the Tiramisu framework, which offers several distinct advantages. It enables real-time IBI assessment, tolerates noisy input signals, and uniquely calculates both expected IBI and its associated uncertainty. Evaluation using the noisy dataset from the WBC2019 IBI competition demonstrated that this Tiramisu-based method surpasses existing techniques, achieving a significantly lower Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.0745 beats compared to the previous best result of 0.103 beats.

Active matter systems are defined by their self-propelled movement, which stems from internal non-equilibrium mechanisms. A versatile theoretical framework for modeling these active agents is the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) model, where the direction of force and magnitude of activity strength are controlled by a variable $\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{t})$. This paper investigates how spatial variations in activity strength impact the effective memory characteristic ($1/\xi_{\mathrm{eff}}$) in one and two dimensions. While agents confined to 1D follow an identical scaling behavior to those in 2D regarding activity profile $n$, the AOUP exhibits a significantly longer active lifetime in 1D confinement. Consequently, this heightened persistence allows 1D agents to traverse longer distances before becoming thermalized compared to their 2D counterparts.

Introducing HUMBI, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate and test 3D human pose generation from gesture input in multivide settings. While related to existing challenges like those found in the Turing Test 2019, HUMBI uniquely offers rich, annotated 3D skeletal data for its instances, enabling the training of autoregressive models capable of outputting full 3D configurations directly. The dataset comprises 11,000 captured instances representing 100 distinct multivide gestures, each annotated with 16 body joints. These instances were generated by 20 performers executing 100 specific gestures across 20 cameras, with every instance tagged using a set of 100 descriptive attributes. To complement the dataset, we have established a benchmark competition that provides a test set of 1,000 multivide instances lacking 3D joint labels to evaluate participant algorithms.

Current cross-lingual transfer methods face significant hurdles: they often demand strong dependencies on deep learning architectures, require extensive tuning, and struggle with a domain gap between source and target languages. This paper introduces NTD, a framework utilizing neural task representations as language-agnostic features to facilitate model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. The approach represents tasks as weak guidance, obviating the need for a language gap to serve as the primary transfer mechanism. By employing an autoencoder to compress input and output data into a compressed neural task depiction, a language-independent signal is generated. This signal functions as high-level weak guidance for a shared encoder-decoder structure, enabling a single multilingual model to be trained on one language and subsequently deployed for others without linguistic alignment. Experiments on abstractive summarization demonstrate that NTD surpasses existing cross-lingual methods and achieves an approximate 80% reduction in data requirements compared to standard zero-shot multilingual approaches.

The primary objective of video super-resolution (VR) is to recover high-quality, detailed imagery by leveraging complementary information from multiple scales. Recently, extensive research has focused on improving VR performance by integrating spatiotemporal alignment and enhanced transmission mechanisms. Building upon this foundation, BasicVSR++ introduces further advancements through four specific innovations. First, it employs a transmission refinement strategy that utilizes spatially weighted memory features to control feature fusion rates, thereby optimizing both image quality and efficiency. Second, it implements a multi-branch transmission alignment architecture to precisely correct variations in transport means, effectively boosting super-resolution recovery. Third, it adopts a multi-memory feature transmission design to jointly utilize features from all previous video frames, thereby maximizing spatiotemporal information utilization. Fourth, it employs a lightweight memory network to store historical features, ensuring efficient long-term memory access. Extensive experiments confirm that basicVSR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, delivering superior super-resolution results.

Research and commercial efforts in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aim to develop general-purpose agents capable of mastering diverse tasks. However, agents trained on specific tasks often suffer from catastrophic performance drops when introduced to new ones, a phenomenon known as negative transfer. This paper proposes a framework to mitigate such negative transfer across multiple tasks by employing modular systems composed of hierarchically organized skills. The agent selects an appropriate module based on the current task, thereby learning each component independently. We demonstrate that this approach to generalization minimizes negative transfer by providing empirical support through support.

We introduce a framework for analyzing optimal finite-duration heat engines that operate under restricted control constraints, applicable to both linear and nonlinear stochastic systems. Our work establishes existence theorems for optimal protocols, develops a variational approach to characterize their features, and, within the linear context, demonstrates that optimal strategies typically align with either the system's maximum allowed control limit or its average power output. notably, these optimal protocols often deviate from standard procedures that simply average power and duration. Furthermore, by examining how power fluctuates, we reveal that their relative fluctuations universally adhere to an extended uncertainty relation that links power, duration, and the system's degrees of freedom.

Severe storms represent the most significant natural threat to power systems, causing the disruption of both power supply and demand as well as damaging infrastructure. This paper analyzes the impact of extreme weather events on the supply, demand, and the physical network, specifically examining the effects on the Texas energy market through a statistical framework. The study evaluates spatio-temporal variations in before-and-after storm scenarios using step-dummy variables to capture distinct pre- and post-hurricane states, alongside interaction terms that vary according to the time elapsed since the event. Results indicate that hurricanes exert measurable impacts across supply, demand, and price levels, with prices showing a stronger reaction than shifts in supply or demand. These imbalances in supply and demand subsequently affect prices in a spatio-temporally heterogeneous manner. Furthermore, the author develops an econometric model to simulate hurricane impacts and integrates this with a Markov Chain framework to represent weather-dependent demand shocks. This approach allows for the construction of a simulation capable of evaluating the efficacy of policy interventions designed to mitigate demand variations during and following severe weather.

This study presents three key results analogous to three-spheres theorems for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator within Clifford-valued functions. The first two uniqueness theorems establish that if such an eigenfunction vanishes on a specific hypersurface within a domain, its values outside that surface can be expressed as an integral incorporating Dirlet kernels. Subsequently, we derive a three-spheres theorem for these eigenfunctions and apply it to produce an analytic-type estimate for their gradients. The final section extends these findings to eigenspinors, which are real-part eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator restricted to Clifford polynomials with real coefficients.

The investigation of non-attracting fractal sets through lens of dynamical systems has yielded significant insights. This study applies that methodology to understand and characterize heterochaos—sophisticated forms of symbolic chaos marked by multiple Lyapunov exponents. We identify specific heterochaos patterns that generate Baker transformations and derive the exact spectra of exponents for measures supported on these sets. Additionally, we outline a mechanism explaining how certain fractal set constructions in heterochaos scenarios can prevent an entropy approach, thereby restricting system evolution.

The standard model's inability to explain phenomena such as dark matter and anomalies in flavor physics motivates research into new particle sectors. A promising extension involves adding a real scalar, a pseudoscalar, and an even-parity pseudoscalar to the theory. While past studies focused on these particles decaying into standard model boson pairs, new possibilities emerge if they instead decay into pairs of scalars or pseudoscalars. This paper investigates the discovery potential of such scenarios at the Large Hadron Collider and projected machines like the High-Luminosity LHC and muon colliders.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), a novel pitch-conditioned audio synthesis framework. Unlike current neural synthesisers that struggle with high-quality pitch control, QPNet employs a pitch-sensitive module featuring dilated convolutions to process raw waveforms, enabling the generation of pitch-class-specific spectral envelopes. This modular approach combines a Quadrature Phase-Locked Loop (QPLL) with the wave-based network to create smooth pitch and spectral trajectories across the waveform. The resulting hybrid architecture demonstrates a significant capability in producing coherent, pitch-varying sounds.

This study introduces a novel bicluster-based approach to collaborative filtering, designed to overcome the challenges of sparsity, subjective rating quality, and the constraints of user-item locality. The system's architecture is divided into two distinct stages. The initial stage involves constructing user-biclusters and item-biclusters by leveraging the consistency within biclusters to narrow down candidate lists, thereby reducing the impact of locality and sparsity. In the second stage, refined features extracted from the narrowed user lists facilitate a collaborative filtering process that utilizes mean-centered Mean Variance Covariance (MVC) to generate personalized recommendations. Experimental evaluations on two public datasets demonstrate that the method yields superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, specifically showing enhanced accuracy in recommendation generation.

To effectively distinguish Majorana zero-energy peaks from other tunneling spectroscopic features, the study introduces a novel experimental technique. Using a split nanowire setup terminated with resistive (Ohmic) normal leads, the method leverages non-equilibrium electron tunneling. In this regime, a bias voltage applied across the sample induces a bias current concentrated at an energy scale matching the voltage magnitude. The proposed device detects this via a bias-dependent measurement of power dissipated as heat. Notably, the energy density of the resulting peak follows a linear dependence on the bias voltage, a unique signature that sets Majorana zero-energy states apart from spurious peaks generated by experimental flaws. The validity of this approach is confirmed through consistency with theoretical predictions made in a companion study (Phys. Rev. B 102, 054517 (2020)).
